subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF FIVE-DAY 40-HOUR WEEK IN VARIOUS DEPARTMENTS    INCREASE IN POSTAGE RATES

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF FIVE-DAY 40-HOUR WEEK IN VARIOUS DEPARTMENTS    INCREASE IN POSTAGE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that, following consultation with the civil service commission, the departments mainly concerned and the national joint council, the government has decided that the policy of readjusting the working week of operating staffs in the post office, customs and various other operating branches of the public service to the five-day forty-hour week where that is the prevailing practice in the locality, which had been approved and announced in September, will be put into effect April 1 next.
Working arrangements will have to be extensively revised and additional employees recruited and trained before the change can be put into effect, but it is believed that this can be accomplished by the end of March with the co-operation of all concerned in assisting to meet the objective.
The civil service commission has been asked to make recommendations to the government for the extension of this new work week to operating staffs in those localities and those classes of employment where the five-day forty-hour week is the established pattern in business and industry.
This change in working hours will make it necessary to add substantially to the staff of the post office. These additions, following the improvements authorized by parliament for rural mail carriers and the salary increases which went into effect on December 1, will materially increase the cost of operating the postal service.
Like all other public utilities with fixed rates, the post office has already been facing difficulty in the past year or two in meeting steadily rising costs, including increased railway and other transport rates and increased remuneration for its employees.
It is anticipated that there will be a deficit on operating account in the present fiscal year and it will certainly not be possible without some increase in revenue to keep the
operations of the post office on a self-sustaining basis in the new fiscal year when the five-day week adds further to operating costs.
It is the view of the government that the people of Canada expect the post office to pay for its operations out of postal revenues and not out of taxes.
The government has accordingly decided to recommend the following adjustments in first-class postage rates effective April 1, 1954:
1.	A general increase of one cent per ounce over existing rates.
2.	The application of the so-called drop letter rate to rural routes as is now done in city and town deliveries.
3.	The reduction of the domestic air mail rate from 7 to 5 cents, with rates outside Canada unchanged.
While the government naturally regrets the necessity for any increase in postage rates, the proposed increase is much more modest than almost all other increases in prices, wage rates or service and transport charges which have been made in the past seven or eight years.
When the new rates come into effect all first-class mail will be carried by air if air carriage will speed up delivery. Canada already has the most advanced air mail service of any country in the world and this service will be further improved.
The government believes the Canadian people want good postal service and the Postmaster General is accordingly giving notice today of the proposed resolution to the effect that it is expedient to introduce a bill to make the necessary amendments to the Post Office Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF FIVE-DAY 40-HOUR WEEK IN VARIOUS DEPARTMENTS    INCREASE IN POSTAGE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this announcement is the first, I am sure, that most hon. members of the house have heard of this decision. I think that certain observations should be made immediately with regard to a statement such as that which has been presented to the house. With respect to most aspects of government activity where the government enters into the field of business operations, I should think there would be little doubt in the mind of any hon. member that, to whatever extent is possible, such operations should be put on a sound businesslike basis. There are, however, certain considerations

Increase in Postage Rates in connection with mail transportation which it seems to me might well have been given some consideration, even if only by the presentation of a substantive motion in the house, before another advance of this kind was made, and particularly at a time when there is such general complaint about the reduction of postal services and deliveries throughout the country.
Throughout the years the speeding up of business communication, the speeding up of personal communication, the speeding up of human contacts, whether it be by mail, telephone, telegraph or any other means of communication, has in itself been an essential part of the material advancement of society. There are few aspects of our social and business contacts which mean more to our people than the efficient delivery of mail at a cost which is consistent in every way with the general public interest. I would have hoped that before a decision of this kind was made, which creates still further differentials between our own postal costs and those of our neighbours in the United States, we might have had some consideration of the possibility of dealing with this problem in another manner.
One of the interesting things that emerge from the statement now presented by the minister is that the minister obviously does not think that the same principle should apply to the postal service as applies to other public services. Without in any way at the moment arguing the merit or demerit of a proposition that the postal service should carry its cost by the stamps purchased, it is interesting to note that no such argument is made as to radio or with respect to certain other public services which the people of the country want and expect to receive. I grant immediately that in the case of radio there are cultural considerations and also special problems connected with it. I am not sure that there may not also be special considerations that should be borne in mind in connection with the postal services as well.
I think there are in this country many people who have advocated over and over again measures of economy which this government has not been prepared to consider or introduce, and who are not convinced that the first consideration in connection with mail delivery in this country must be that, of necessity, the cost of the stamps pay the full cost. I think the first consideration is the efficiency of the service; the opportunity of those who are serving in the mail service itself to be able to perform their task well; and, on top of that, that in this country of ours there be due consideration to the fact that with mail, as with other services, there


are great areas of the country in which special costs are incurred unless there is to be a disadvantage by virtue alone of living in that area.
Those are all things that present certain special considerations. I simply rise at this moment, Mr. Speaker, without previous knowledge of the fact that this statement was going to be presented, to suggest that this is something that might well be given further consideration. I suggest there ought to be an examination of the whole organization and set-up of the postal service by a committee of this house, so that the hours of work and other details of that kind within the postal service could be examined. We should find out whether those working in the postal service are, in fact, receiving the consideration they should receive for this very valuable service.
There is a question raised by many as to whether the employees are not working excessive hours and under excessive conditions, having regard to the special terms of their employment. I am not making any positive statement in regard to these things, but I do say there are few subjects on which there has been more comment in recent months than the postal service. I would have hoped that before a blanket decision of this kind had been made there would have been an opportunity to examine the postal service, always bearing in mind that the efficiency of that service depends upon the feeling of confidence on the part of postal employees themselves that their services are being fully appreciated and employed to the best advantage.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.

speechtext:
Righl Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 6, respecting the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think hon. members will realize that this bill now before the house is an important one, not so much because of what it contains or does, in precise terms, but because of what its passage will signify. The effect of the bill will not be to establish a new department of government, nor to extend the scope of government in any way, nor even to add new functions to those discharged by the department affected by the bill. The effect of the bill will be rather to give a new emphasis and scope to work already being done, and to indicate that the government and parliament wish to see such greater emphasis made a continuing feature of the operation of government.
One subject to which such increased emphasis will be given by passage of this bill is the administration and development of our northern territories. Perhaps I might say a brief word as background about the administration of those northern territories.
Hon. members will know that in 1870 the United Kingdom transferred to Canada Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories. Rupert's Land at that time included the whole of the watershed of Hudson bay and Hudson strait, and had been under the administration of the Hudson's Bay Company since it obtained its original charter in 1670 [DOT]-that is, something over 200 years ago.
The Northwest Territories-or the Northwest Territory, because it was all one territory-comprised the vast region between Rupert's Land on the east and British Columbia and Alaska on the west. When these lands were transferred to Canada the department of the interior was set up to handle their administration, and in the same year, 1870, the province of Manitoba was carved out of the new lands added to the extent of Canada. The administration of the remainder continued under the department of the interior, though the active administration in the territory was in the hands of a lieutenant governor and an appointed council.
I do not want to go into the history of this form of government, but I might mention a few of the highlights of that period. In 1888 there was a first session of a partly elected legislative assembly for the territory. In 1897 responsible government was seriously fMr. Knowles.]
considered for the territories, but subject to the overriding control of the department of the interior and of the governor general in council.
In 1898 the Yukon Territory was separated from the Northwest Territories, and a separate organization was set up for the administration of its local affairs. That was probably the result of the growth of population in the Klondike at that time, as a consequence of the gold rush.
In 1905 the two provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were created by acts of this parliament. Then, in 1912, the northern boundaries of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba were extended to their present limits, and that took in a large part of the former Northwest Territories. Thus, by 1912 the northern territories of Canada had assumed their present limits and comprised practically all the lands north of the sixtieth degree north latitude, except a small portion of Quebec, which extends into the Ungava district beyond the sixtieth parallel and a small portion of the Newfoundland territory as well. The territories had, as they have today, administrations of their own different from that of the Yukon Territory; but the control of the administration continued to be in the department of the interior.
In 1936, as part of an economy measure, four departments of government were merged to form the department of mines and resources, and one of those four was the department of the interior, and the administration of the north country became one of the many duties of the department of mines and resources. Hon. members know that that department had the administration of mines, of immigration, of mapping and surveys, of Indian affairs, of national parks, of forest resources and so forth, and it was not possible that very much of the attention of the department could be given specifically to northern affairs.
After 1945 it became clear that the department of mines and resources had activities too varied and too numerous, and there was a need for rearrangement of functions. That department was replaced by three new departments. Immigration and Indian affairs, plus citizenship, which up to that time had been the responsibility of the Secretary of State, became the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The duties in respect of mines, mapping, and surveys were grouped under the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The other functions of the former department of mines and resources made the third department of Resources and Development. Thus in 1950 the administration of the

northern territories passed to the Department of Resources and Development. But that department had many other duties as well. It was in charge of the forest resources that belonged to the national government, irrigation and water power development, national parks, wildlife generally, historic sites and monuments, the national museum, the tourist services, trans-Canada highway and so forth, and the minister was also the minister to whom the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the film board reported, and through whom their reports were communicated to parliament.
It has seemed to us that with that set-up it was obvious that northern affairs could get only a part, and perhaps a rather small part, of the attention of the minister and of the department, and it was also apparent that throughout the whole history of the administration of our territories there had never been a department clearly charged with their administration as its first and primary duty.
Now, it seemed to us that it was becoming increasingly apparent that it would be desirable to alter the situation and to create conditions in which it is clearly indicated that the government and parliament want further attention given to the development of our north country, and I may say that that was further impressed upon us by the fact that there have to be quite a number of non-Canadians going into that territory. We felt that it was very important to have the situation such that whenever they went there they realized they were in Canadian territory and in territory that was administered by Canadian authorities.
The present bill is designed to give more emphasis to the fact that the people of Canada are greatly interested in this northern territory and regard it as an important part of the territory subject to the sovereignty of the Canadian nation. The purpose of this bill is to further that objective. The first step was taken in September 1953, when certain duties of the Minister of Resources and Development were transferred to other ministers. Housing, trans-Canada highway, planning of special projects were all transferred to the Minister of Public Works. The national film board was transferred to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Thus the minister and the Department of Resources and Development were relieved of some of the duties that do not relate to our north country; but it has seemed to us that the other remaining duties could well be corollaries of the principal duty emphasized by the act of administering the interest of the Canadian people in our northern territory.
Northern Affairs and National Resources
The government is now recommending to the house a redefinition of the duties of the department and a shift of emphasis and a new name. We think that the new name is rather important; it is indicative of the fact that the centre of gravity of the department is being moved north. That is the purpose of this measure. The Department of Resources and Development will become the department of northern affairs and national resources. It is quite proper that they should be together because the national resources subject to the jurisdiction of parliament and vested in Her Majesty in the right of Canada are the resources that are situated in the northern territories. All those that are in the older provinces, the original provinces, were vested in the Queen in the right of the provincial governments at confederation. When British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island- in the case of Prince Edward Island there was no difficulty-and when the prairie provinces were established, the natural resources were retained. Hon. members will remember that that was a bone of contention for a long time between the federal authorities and the provincial authorities. They have now been surrendered to the provincial authorities and are vested in Her Majesty in the right of the respective provinces. The natural resources of Canada are now the natural resources in the territories that are outside those of provincial administration.
This will be .the first time that this designation "northern affairs" will have appeared in the name of a department of the government of Canada. I hope it will be felt, as we felt, that it is desirable that this be done as one of the indications of the growing interest in the importance of these northern territories. The functions of the department will remain essentially the same as those of the department of resources, except that hereafter responsibilities in relation to the north will be more fully and clearly spelled out. The minister will have the specific duty to co-ordinate the activities of all government departments in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. It will also be his responsibility to promote measures for further economic and political development in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and to develop knowledge of the problems in .the north and the means of dealing with them through scientific investigations and technological research. *
I think it is rather fortunate to have the occasion presented by this bill, one that is perhaps too rare, to do something in the nature of national stocktaking. Occasions do not occur very frequently. We are usually too deeply involved in the urgent day to
698	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources day problems to take time off to do that, but it would seem that occasionally it is desirable to step back and to see where we are and how we are getting on and where we are going.
There have been some of these occasions during the time I have been in the house. There was such an occasion when the house debated the Canadian Citizenship Act in 1946; when it debated the United Nations agreements also in 1946; and when we had the interesting debate over the union of Newfoundland with Canada in 1949. There have been other cases; and then at every session we have general debates on trade, agriculture, broadcasting and shipping.
But there has not been for a long time any special occasion offered to discuss these vast areas of Canada which compose the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory. It has been said that Great Britain acquired her empire in a state of absence of mind. Apparently we have administered these vast territories of the north in an almost continuing state of absence of mind.
I think all hon. members now feel that the territories are vastly important to Canada and that it is time that more attention was focused upon their possibilities and what they will mean to this Canadian nation. We in the southern part of Canada have been so busy in recent years that we have given little close attention to the north country. In the thirties we were concerned with economic problems; then during the war years there was little that we could devote ourselves to but to the tasks of war. Since the war the growth and development in every province and the problems of the cold war have absorbed practically the whole of our attention.
The extent to which some of us are unaware of the north was brought home to me personally a few weeks ago. We were receiving a delegation which had set up in the room in which they were being received a large map of North America. I was looking at the map and it struck me that Alaska looked to be larger than Ontario. I said, "I am not saying that this map is not accurate but it must be drawn in such a way as to throw the northern portion out of perspective with the rest". However, on checking it I found to my surprise that in fact Alaska is larger in area than the whole of Ontario even with its augmented boundaries. It is just a trifle smaller than Quebec, which reaches almost up to the north pole with its extended boundaries.
There may be others who have the same concept that I had that these northern areas,

although very vast, are not of the extent which on checking one finds them to be. The Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory together have an area of 1,511,979 square miles. The total area of Canada, including the territories, is 3,847,774 square miles. The Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory constitute 39-3 per cent of the total.
The area of the Yukon Territory is 207,076 square miles, nearly as large as any one of the three prairie provinces. Taking the three districts of the Northwest Territories, Mackenzie district, the most westward, has an area of 527,490 square miles; Keewatin, which is west of Hudson bay, has an area of 228,160 square miles; and Franklin, or the islands of the Arctic, has an area of about 550,000 square miles. Mackenzie and Franklin are each larger than any province in Canada except Quebec with the northern extension which it got in 1912.
Of course the population of the territories is still small in relation to their area, but it is growing percentagewise quite rapidly. It is a healthy growth based upon proven resources that are being used and are providing a livelihood for the population. In 1941 the population of the Yukon was just about 5,000; in 1951 it was around 9,000. In 1941 the population of Whitehorse was 754; according to the 1951 census it had a population of 2,594.
The growth in the Northwest Territories themselves is also quite striking. The population in 1941 was 12,000; in 1951 it was 16,000. The population other than Indian and Eskimo in 1941 was 2,290; in 1951 it was 5,344. The growth and development of the territories is perhaps somewhat reminiscent of what took place in the Canadian west at the end of the last century. They have not yet reached the stage of full bloom which occurred when the west filled up in the early years of the century, but they have reached a stage where it is clear that the north, just as certainly as had the west fifty years ago, has a great future for the benefit of the Canadian nation.
Of course, it will not be the same kind of a future that brought about the rapid development of the prairie provinces where the principal resource that could be exploited was agriculture.
In the north the basic industry for growth and development is mining, and important discoveries have already taken place; and in the Yukon gold is still a commodity of importance. In 1952 the amount of gold produced, according to the bureau of statistics, was of the value of $2,700,000, and silver and base metals were also produced in increasing volume and value. In 1952 the

value of silver mined in the Yukon was $3,300,000; lead, $2,950,000; zinc, $1,900,000. In the Northwest Territories the value of gold grew from $1,800,000 in 1939 to $8,-
400,000	in 1952.
We all know that discoveries of uranium are of the greatest importance economically, and also have political significance. Petroleum and silver have been found in encouraging amounts at various points, and I think that the developments so far are an indication of what we might expect in the future in regard to these northern areas.
I am not a geologist, but I am told that the largest part of the Northwest Territories is made up of ancient rock of the preCambrian shield, and all of the eastern and central mainland and much of Baffin island as well, while the western edge of the Northwest Territories and all of the Yukon lie across the Cordilleras. The Pre-Cambrian shield and the Cordilleras are, I am told, the two great metal-bearing regions of North America. The Mackenzie basin is an extension of the central plains and it is well known that oil discoveries have been made in that region, and it is coming to be regarded by many, who I hope are not overenthusiastic, as the great oil-bearing region of North America.
Up to the present, development has been held up by the remoteness of the area, the problem of transportation, the rigorous nature of the climate, and the toughness of the terrain; but from what I know of the geology of the territories, and what has been learned by experts, the resources there are sufficient to give confidence that the present output will be quite dwarfed by the developments of the future. We know that at the present time in parts of Canada, some of which are perhaps less remote and less difficult of access, great new wealth is being discovered.
I had the advantage at the end of last summer of visiting Knob Lake in Labrador, and the Ungava district, 360 or 370 miles north of Seven Islands, and I felt I was pretty far north. But the territories beyond that are greater than what is between that place and the latitude of Seven Islands. I was astounded at the work that is being done there to take out ten million tons of iron ore a year. That means ten million tons in six months because the season does not last beyond that period. Of course that development would have been quite impossible without the use of air transportation. Machines had to be brought in in order to do anything at all and a railway of 370 miles was being completed from Seven Islands to the mineral deposits. There are other interesting deposits in that
Northern Affairs and National Resources same region, and there is abundant water power. Natural conditions in the territories are such as to make anyone who is at all optimistic feel that there is a great future for this Canada of ours because of the tremendous extent of its territory and the natural resources with which it has been so generously endowed.
I am told that over $2 million worth of fish annually is being taken out of Great Slave lake at the present time. This fish was trucked to the railhead and shipped to Chicago. The hydroelectric possibilities of the region are immense. By the construction of dams at appropriate places, some of them reversing the flow of certain rivers and lakes draining into the Yukon river, and by taking advantage of the large drop of the level of that country to the Pacific, power can be developed in enormous quantities. It was suggested to me that there was more than 4 i million horsepower that could be developed in that way. Hon. members will remember that some time ago there was a suggestion that these waters, or much of them, could be diverted for development into Alaska. Well, they are Canadian waters and while we do not want to adopt any dog in the manger attitude about our resources which cannot be used in our own country, I think that those which can be used in our country must be reserved for the generations that will follow us and who will develop this country. I was happy that the minister's declaration in that regard was applauded in the house on December 17, 1952, and I am glad to see that my reference to it today meets with the unanimous approval of the representatives of all the Canadian people. We do not want to be isolationists but we do feel we have a trust to future generations for the resources with which Providence has endowed this vast land over which now our people exercise sovereignty.
There is another aspect which makes it necessary for us to give more attention to these northern territories and that is the fact that the Canadian northland lies between the two greatest powers in the world at the present time, namely, the United States of America and the U.S.S.R., and our own security is probably made more difficult to provide for by the fact that this northland of ours is between these two great world powers. There will, no doubt, have to be joint measures taken for the security of the North American continent. It is a continental problem that presents itself for solution by that mere fact of geography. I am not going to say any more about it than was said by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), but all these joint undertakings are
700	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources carried out under the principle which the President enunciated from the head of the table here only three or four weeks ago. They are implemented with full respect for the sovereignty of the country in which they are carried out.
We must leave no doubt about our active occupation and exercise of our sovereignty in these northern lands right up to the pole. That is something which puts these lands in a somewhat different position from other parts of Canada. From other parts of Canada we get representations from the localities about the things that are required for their development. Here I think there must be someone having ministerial responsibility to take initiatives so we will not have to wait until there are representations from the so sparse population in the area as to what is required. It was for these reasons that it was held it would be desirable to have on the statute books a department of northern affairs and to have representatives of the department of northern affairs present in various parts of these territories and symbolic of the actuality of the exercise of Canadian sovereignty over them.
There is another aspect, too. I have been quite impressed by what I have read and seen in films about the Eskimos. They seem to be a very sympathetic group of people. I understand there is a young Eskimo attending university in Calgary now who is taking technical and engineering training and showing that he is an outstanding pupil. I think this department will have to give close attention to what can be done to integrate the native Eskimo population into the development, and probably the administration also, of parts of these northern areas.
Having a demonstration of what they can do, it is probably a responsibility that the Canadian people would want to have their government discharge to provide them with opportunities for developing their talents and making themselves real citizens of the Canadian nation. It is for all these reasons that it has been felt that it would be desirable to have an energetic young minister be conscious that his principal responsibility will be to devote his attention to the northern affairs of this nation in that area which is 40 per cent of the area of the whole of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was particularly interested in listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to hear him reiterate what I think are the two salient points of government policy. The first is that water power and the development thereof in Canada shall remain


for the benefit of Canada. The second point is that the present administration, although in my opinion somewhat belatedly, is looking to the north.
This is an omnibus bill. It is a somewhat smaller omnibus than it was before, and as such I welcome it. But it shows what happens in a government when it gets into so many activities. I suppose that this is a bit difficult to avoid, but it seems that such matters as the tourist trade and the national museum are slightly out of place in a department of northern development, although in part they do depend on the north. The tourist trade depends on the north to attract tourists to Canada, although not the north as we are referring to it in this instance, and no doubt the geological section of the national museum has many specimens from the north. However, I point out that neither the tourist trade nor the national museum is really a part of northern affairs.
As I have said, this bill is a simplification and as such I welcome it. Dealing with the first point in the bill, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, as the Prime Minister pointed out, these regions consist of the Cordilleras, which are of course the Rocky mountains, the Pre-Cambrian shield and the area of the great plains. All of these areas are host to minerals. They are probably the greatest host to minerals to be found anywhere in the world today. The development of those minerals is a challenge which this and succeeding generations of Canadians will have to meet if our nation is to prosper and remain a sovereign state even in the way it has up to now. I say that with the utmost seriousness because I do not know whether hon. members are aware of what has happened in the rest of the world, and more particularly in the United States, with regard to the exhaustion of natural resources.
It may astound some hon. members when I say that as far as metals are concerned the United States is at present self-sufficient only in magnesium and molybdenum, and as magnesium is obtainable from sea water through a certain process it is a mineral in which any country can be self-sufficient. So we see that the United States, the great leader of western civilization, the nation whose prosperity has been built on the resources of iron, coal and petroleum, is today in a deficient position. I have here a pamphlet containing an address by a very eminent Canadian, one to whom every Canadian should be deeply indebted. I refer to Dr. George Sherwood Hume, O.B.E. He addressed the geological association of Canada at its sixth annual meeting; and while I will not go into these

matters in detail I do want to point out the have-not position of the United States at the present time with respect to so many minerals, and the challenge that presents to us in Canada. I shall quote this one short paragraph:
In former times much of the requirements of the United States was produced within the borders of that country which, with less than 10 per cent of the free world's population and 8 per cent of its land area, consumes close to half the free world's volume of materials. But far from being wholly self-sustaining, the United States is now the world's largest importer of copper, lead and zinc. The United States also imports considerable amounts of petroleum and iron ore, as well as most other minerals.
Dr. Hume then refers to the now famous Paley report in these words:
It is pointed out in the Paley report that the countries with undeveloped resources do not look with favour on the total exportation of raw materials to be processed by the importing countries. That sentiment certainly exists to some extent, and rightly so, in Canada and the Paley report clearly recognizes the fact that in the United States, as a seller, the emphasis shifted from raw materials to manufactured goods, and as a buyer from finished goods to raw materials. Thus a certain amount of processing of raw materials in the country of origin is not an unreasonable position for the exporting country to assume.
Now, in the language of one of our best known geologists, that means we have to be prepared to do more of the processing and developing of our natural resources in Canada. I do not want to hark back to the days of 1911 when an election was won on the slogan that Canadians were going to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the United States. Dr. Hume says virtually the same thing, in reverse. This means, Mr. Speaker, that the great mineral resources in the Yukon and Northwest Territories must be processed at least in part in Canada.
The processing of these materials requires one thing predominantly, and that is primary power. I am pleased to hear the government reiterate the fact that it is basic Canadian policy, and speaking as a Conservative I assure you that it is basic Conservative policy, that we will not export primary power which we need in Canada. I hope to show this house that we do need every kilowatt hour of power that we can possibly produce.
I should like to compare two recent major developments. The first is the Alcan project in British Columbia, and I am using it as an example to show what is possible on another project in the Yukon. In connection with the Alcan project it is estimated that by diverting a river through a tunnel which goes through the coast range, and dropping to tide water, a million and a half horsepower can be generated. This power will produce 80,000 metric tons of aluminum per
Northern Affairs and National Resources annum, will result in the establishment of Kitimat, a town of some 35,000 people within less than a decade, and require a capital expenditure of about $500 million, all of which is being raised by private enterprise. Now, that is a stupendous undertaking.
A little farther north, at Tulsequah, by diverting the Yukon river by a somewhat similar engineering feat, through tunnels down to sea level at Taku inlet, approximately 5-5 million horsepower can be developed. That is potential energy greater than exists on the entire St. Lawrence seaway and Niagara river together. The industrial heart of Canada, the cities of Toronto and Montreal, all the industries which we know in that section, were built upon the primary power in the Niagara and St. Lawrence areas. These industries came into being because of the abundance of cheap electric power. Canada has not been a fuel-rich country, except in the last few years owing to the discovery of oil and gas. Each of these two developments approximately equals the primary power which built industrial Canada.
In this same area we have a potential in minerals, the extent of which is only vaguely understood despite years of prospecting and all the modern tools which have been produced to aid prospecting. With this and the power we have in this area, at least in part, the answer to the have-not position of the United States. This is a challenge which we cannot afford to let pass. It must be met, otherwise our economy will remain a small adjunct of the United States economy. I mention that, Mr. Speaker, to show how important I consider this development really is. Over the next quarter century it could, in the main, be the answer to our international balance of payments.
We now know metals do exist at places like Arch Creek near Kluane lake where new deposits of nickel and copper have recently been discovered which also contain precious metals. The St. Elias range in the Selwyn mountains is known to contain iron in considerable quantities. The recent discoveries this summer of lead and zinc are also important, but we have merely scratched the surface of the area which will be served by this vast hydroelectric source of energy.
So much for the primary development. Now let us look at the reason why North America has been prosperous. We have been able to pay our workers high wages. We have been able to live in what people who are not on the North American continent consider to be a state of absolute luxury. We have our motor cars, houses, ample food, cheap clothes and

Northern Affairs and National Resources hundred of thousands of miles of good roads, all those things which the non-North American considers great luxuries.
What is the reason for this? The reason is that we have been able to provide our workers and ourselves with power and tools. I would show here the way in which electrical energy at the hands of industrial workers has increased since 1929. In that year the worker in the industrial part of North America used 2.61 kilowatts of energy per man-hour. This had increased in 1939 to 4.60, in 1940 to 5.71 and in 1950 to 6.29. It is estimated that at the present time the figure has reached almost 8 kilowatts per man-hour.
That is a staggering increase in the use of energy; but it, together with the machine it drives, more than anything else stand as the reason we have been able to maintain our prosperity in the face of low wages, cheap materials and all other threats from abroad. We and the Americans have been able to export throughout the world simply because we have had this abundant source of electrical energy. This we must not jeopardize.
In our basic industries in Canada the use of electrical energy is, of course, very considerably greater than the figure I have placed on record. The 8 kilowatts might be multiplied many times over; and in some industries such as the aluminum industry, it might be multiplied many hundreds of times per man-hour. Therefore this source of electrical energy is of vital importance to us.
I do not propose to say anything about Eskimo affairs, except that the Eskimo is not an Indian, and must be treated differently. He lives in a different part of the world.
I notice the bill makes reference to the forest and water resources of Canada, and I assume it refers only to those forest and water resources which are not within provincial jurisdiction. Therefore I should think that this bill will not require any alterations in the terms of the British North America Act.
The subject of national parks has been dealt with in another bill, but I am glad to see it in the omnibus legislation before us. There is also in the bill reference to historic places and monuments, also a subject dealt with in another bill.
Then we see reference to the archaeology, ethnology and fauna and flora of Canada, as well as reference to the national museum. I should like to mention briefly some of the problems which present themselves in connection with the national museum. I would say that it is in a most unsatisfactory state in that it is too small and is crowded with people and things from other departments.

Many of the exhibits are crated and hidden away, and they must remain so for years to come. I hope that when the federal plan for the beautification of Ottawa is fully developed one of the first projects will be adequate provision for the proper housing of a national museum, separate and apart altogether from the art gallery.
There is one other point I would mention, and which might be classified either in the subject of ethnology or in that of historic places and monuments. I refer to the decay on the Pacific coast of the totem poles, something which I consider nothing less than a disgrace. The modern Indian is not interested in the traditions and history signified by the totem pole. The result is that many of these historic monuments-for that is what they are-are now lying rotting, or in a state of decay. These are found all up and down the Pacific coast. I would sincerely hope that one of the first acts of the new minister would be to see that these relics of our history, because that is what they are, might be restored, or at least that there might be preservation of those parts remaining.
Then I find here reference to the tourist industry, and I would hope that in that connection there might be a greater national appeal. It seems to me that the average tourist, particularly from the United States, can leave that country, pass through minor formalities at the frontier, and spend a week or two in Canada without ever realizing that he is in another country. There comes to mind little things like the flying of the stars and stripes rather than the Canadian flag at tourist resorts. I think anyone touring this country should be impressed by the national characteristics and life of the country. I realize that this is not something to be legislated for, but certainly it can be encouraged. When a visitor comes to Canada he should be made to feel that he is in another country; that we are Canadians; that we have a definite, specific national life and we are Canadians, not merely Americans living across an invisible line. There are many ways of doing that; but I just venture to say that that would be one of the things that would make tourist travel in Canada at least distinctive, which it is not at the present time.
I should also like to see the encouragement of things like the Shakespearean festival at Stratford and perhaps the summer symphonies, which could make this country alive for the tourists to see, and not merely endless roads, excellent as they are in many ways but not distinguishable from roads in any United States state.

Before I close I want to mention one further thing, because this bill deals with irrigation. At the present time the world is suffering from a food famine. One would not believe it, listening to debates here in which are mentioned hundreds of millions of bushels of wheat in storage without any market for them. Nevertheless the world is suffering from a famine. There are more people with not enough to eat today than at any time in the present century. I think I am safe in saying that. The growth of the population has brought that about.
Sir Dudley Stamp, who was the director of food production in the United Kingdom during the war, and who at one time was professor of agronomy at either Wisconsin or Minnesota, has, with the help of the world food organization, shown that the greatest potential increase in the production of food is in the great plains area of North America. We have not considered this to be as important as we might because we have been bedevilled with the problem, and we still are bedevilled with the problem, of finding a market for our surplus food. Nevertheless, if we are to endeavour to be citizens of the world, there is a problem which we must face, namely, the finding of ways in which to produce and market the increase of food which the great plains can and will produce. It is a matter that I will not go into at this moment because it concerns the delicate subject of the convertibility of currency. Nevertheless it does present a challenge to us in Canada.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I welcome this bill. I wish the new minister well in his department. I hope that his annual reports will tell a story of production and development as substantial as I optimistically believe the situation warrants.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was particularly pleased, in listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to hear him state that this gave the house an opportunity for a national stocktaking; for it seems to me that is an undertaking that is long overdue and it is something in the nature of a national stocktaking that I wish to undertake this afternoon.
In British Columbia we are particularly interested in the development of the northern territories, owing to our close association with the Yukon Territory and to the fact also that from the ports of British Columbia go many of the ships that traverse the northern coasts of this continent. We are also interested in this bill from another point of view, namely, that in British Columbia we have had, possibly not alone, among districts in
Northern Affairs and National Resources Canada, some unfortunate experiences in the past with measures taken in previous years for the development of our resources.
We have a long history of expropriation, shall we say, of resources by private individuals with the aid and the help of past governments and parliaments. We have in the area which I represent in this house one of the most striking examples of that perhaps in the whole of Canada. I refer to the notorious-and I use the word "notorious" advisedly-Esquimalt and Nanaimo land grant, whereby a grant of a quarter of the whole of Vancouver island was given to a group of enterprising gentlemen as a subsidy or part of a subsidy for the building of 70 miles of railroad, and in addition they got some $750,000 in cash and very valuable tax exemption privileges.
In British Columbia we do not forget that, because we come up against it every day in our provincial and in our local financial problems. These tax exempt privileges are now a burden on the people of that part of British Columbia. We have had also in more recent times in British Columbia a development, perhaps one of the new methods, by which private enterprise manages to dig its fingers into the public pocket. We have on Vancouver island now the site of a large publicly-owned hydroelectric development, and it is interesting because of the circumstances which surround that particular development in my province. It was developed ostensibly for the purpose of bringing cheap electrical power to rural areas, to the farm and to the rural homes of Vancouver island. It was only later of course that it became plain that this large investment of public funds had been undertaken for the prime and sole purpose of pro viding very cheap power for one particular interest, to such an extent, sir, that the rates charged to that corporation which were divulged only a year or two ago-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this bill I would like to say, as a new member, that in listening to some of the speeches made in this house I often wonder whether these speeches are intended to be a demonstration of the respective members' speaking ability or are a sincere attempt to contribute something to the debate.
I must confess I am not an excellent speaker, but I hope to be able to contribute to this debate something that will be of value to members of this house and also of assistance to those who are charged with the responsibility of developing our northern resources.
I think the greatest aid to development is the provision of communications, the railways, highways and telephone systems which I think are required more than anything else at this time in order to assist this projected development. We have found in the past that capital has been available for the development of areas where ample communication services were available. It seems to me that wherever we have provided these services people have been prepared to go into such places. If people can have a fairly respectable living and decent conditions they are only too willing to pioneer. Possibly I come
[Mr. Macdonnell.l

from a pioneering family. I lived in a land of promises where we were promised things for 30 or 40 years and they never came.
There are various matters that should be taken into consideration so far as northern development is concerned, and I am going to refer particularly to the area which I represent because the development of the northern part of Canada and the Yukon is directly related to that of the part of British Columbia from which I come. First of all I want to mention the highway situation. There should be co-operation between this department which we are now creating, the Department of National Defence and the Department of Public Works, as hinted in the Prime Minister's address a short while ago. In order to have development we must have co-ordination of the efforts of these various departments. Too often we find that we have isolated the different departments too well, and that there is not enough dovetailing of effort to secure the most for the taxpayer's dollar.
There is a new highway that runs right through my riding from north to south. It enters the riding at Marguerite and a thousand miles to the north passes into the Yukon at Lower Post. This is an arterial highway in the province of British Columbia which carries traffic from the United States to Alaska, passing through the Yukon. I consider that as an arterial highway it deserves the consideration of the federal government with respect to support. I am not suggesting how this is to be accomplished or how much the support should be; I am only saying that in my opinion financial support should be extended.
There is another matter which is directly concerned with northern development, and that is the development of highways in Canada on the basis of their classification as arterial highways. I suggest that they should be so classified and that federal support should be granted on that basis. Telephone communications should naturally follow the development of our highways. On our highways we find that we have the ribbon development that is so necessary to take care of travellers passing back and forth over these roads.
I am not going to take much more time. I should like to mention the railway situation. There is a railway running from Squamish at the present time-and we hope in the not too distant future it will be extended to Vancouver-north as far as Prince George. I think it is essential that the departments of the federal government and the provincial government co-operate with respect to pushing railroads northward

from Prince George, and perhaps also from Dawson Creek or Hines Creek through the Peace pass to Finlay Forks and thence north to the Yukon with a connecting link to Hazelton and Prince George.
Without seeing these places on a map it is rather difficult for hon. members to visualize exactly what I am speaking about, but those who are interested only have to glance at a map to realize that this is an important step in the development of the north country.
There is only one more point I wish to make. I do not know whether this bill will be the means of making provision for the reclamation and recognition of historic places, but I should like to say that I believe at one time Barkerville was the largest city west of Chicago. Today there are many historic buildings in Barkerville which should receive some consideration if it is within the scope of this measure to do so.
That is all I have to say at this time. I know there are other speakers who have a great deal to contribute to the debate. I certainly appreciate the time afforded to me, and I hope that when the matters I have mentioned are examined it will be found that in some way I have contributed to this debate.

Northern Affairs and National Resources the Yukon in any sound measures he undertakes for the further economic and political development of the Yukon Territory, and I hope he will take into consideration the views and experience of the people who have spent a lifetime in the Yukon.
The economic development of the north is primarily dependent upon the development of its mineral resources, and the people are looking to the government to provide encouragement and help. The development of other resources such as water power, lands, forests and so on will follow and be dependent upon the development of its minerals. When our two great natural resources, minerals and water power, are brought together, great developments that contribute to the welfare of the Yukon and of Canada generally are possible. I feel gratified, consequently, that this fact has been recognized by various mining and development companies which have been investigating in the field the mineral and power potential of the Yukon Territory and northern British Columbia. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that great progress has been made to date.
I suggest the policy in regard to this vast enterprise, now in its early stages, should be one of energy and vision with the realization that here is an opportunity to really develop the Yukon Territory. I do not doubt the government fully realizes the possibilities. I have every confidence that the minister will have ample opportunity to display vision in formulating plans for the development of these resources. I hope also, Mr. Speaker, that he will be blessed with the same vision the fathers of confederation had when they laid the plans which cemented the widely scattered provinces into this nation of which we are so proud.
It is not so long ago since we were pushing our frontiers to the west, but our new frontier is now to the north. It is in that direction we must now face, and it is this frontier that we must roll back so Canada will have depth as well as breadth. The opening of the west was accelerated by the provision of transportation and communication facilities. The provision of these facilities was not left entirely to private enterprise, but was assisted in varying ways by the federal government.
We all know that the improvement of communications in any part of Canada helps to bind our country together, to make us more united and to speed up the development of our great resources. There is no part of Canada where transportation and communication are more vital than in the Yukon and in the north country generally. The economic development of the north will be encouraged and accelerated by the provision of these
708	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources facilities. The area of the north is so vast, and the distance is so great, that it would seem only wise for the federal government to assume a much greater share of the burden in providing these essential facilities and services.
I am sure we all agree, Mr. Speaker, that one way of ensuring a period of prosperity and development for the next century would be to embark on a wholesale development of our northern heritage. There is a job to be done in the Yukon and Northwest Territories for the benefit of this and future generations, so we may reap the harvest of our northern inheritance.
Section 6 of the bill delegates responsibility to the minister to undertake and promote measures for the further economic development of the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
At this time I should like to briefly mention some of the more important projects which, in my opinion, would contribute to the immediate economic development of the Yukon territory. I hope that at another time I may have the opportunity of enlarging on the benefits of these projects, but at the moment I shall only mention them briefly.
They are the construction of an all-weather road from Dawson westward to the Yukon-Alaska boundary to connect with the existing highway system in Alaska and the Alaska highway; improvement of the road from Stewart Crossing to Dawson to the same standard as the Whitehorse-Mayo road; construction of permanent bridges along the Whitehorse-Mayo road to replace the ferries; construction of an all-weather road from Mayo northward to tap the rich mineral resources known to exist in the watersheds of the Beaver and Peel rivers; participation in the construction of an all-weather road from Carcross, Yukon to tidewater at Skagway, Alaska; rehabilitation of the Canol road in the Yukon; expansion of stream measurement programs to encourage hydroelectric development; improvement of the presently hazardous airfields at Dawson and Mayo to provide safer runways and modern flying facilities; construction of a radio station powerful enough to provide news and cultural programs to all people in the Yukon Territory, such as are now enjoyed by people in less remote parts of Canada; construction of a railway from Prince George, British Columbia northward through the Rocky mountain trench into the Yukon and thence to Alaska.
There are other important projects which I shall not mention at this time. Section 6 of the bill, Mr. Speaker, also delegates to the minister responsibility for planning


and promoting measures for the further political development of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. As the population increases with the growing economic development there will undoubtedly have to be a parallel development of the political institutions of the territory. We have experienced representative government in the Yukon for well over 50 years. With the great development and the increasing population we will experience in the next few years, the time will then be ripe to provide a further step in constitutional development, so the executive will be responsible to the territorial legislature which has been accepting the responsibility without a corresponding right of control. X feel confident that a large measure of selfgovernment will naturally follow.
I am pleased to say that the present financial arrangement between the Yukon government and the federal government has led to a better understanding between the two governments, but it does not take sufficiently into account the accelerated tempo of development which we are now experiencing in the Yukon Territory. It is to be hoped that this agreement will be amended to provide for more generous recognition of the true situation. I certainly hope the minister and the deputy minister will pay a visit to the Yukon this summer. I can assure them that they will be welcomed by all Yukoners.
I wish to express my appreciation also of the Prime Minister's action in creating this department to deal with northern affairs. He has shown farsightedness and a sound and sympathetic human reaction to the often unexpressed but deep feeling of the people of our north country. The signs of the times appear to justify Laurier's forecast that the twentieth century shall be a century of Canada and of Canadian development. Let us approach the question of developing our northern frontiers in the earnest and candid spirit of men bound by the same interests, seeking the same common end, and loving the same country.

speechtext:
Less than half an hour ago the President of the United States of America completed one of the most significant speeches of our time. It is a speech which should offer greater encouragement than the people of this world have had for many years. The fact that it was so clearly a speech which represented the united opinions of the United States, Great Britain and France gives it a significance and meaning that should reach the heart of every person in this world,

whether beyond the iron curtain or on this side of it, who looks toward that day of peace for which we have all been hoping.
I mention this because that speech in many ways was directly related to the subject matter of the bill now before us, which has to do with the possibilities of that immense area within which was first discovered on this North American continent the fissionable material from which such destructive forces have been built as part of the common defence of freedom throughout these past years.
After having reviewed the terrifying increase in the power of atomic weapons which find their source in minerals which have been discovered in abundance in our own north country, the President placed before the United Nations and the world proposals for a peaceful solution of this terrifying problem, which could mean not only the fulfilment of the hope of peace but could also mean an entirely new concept of the importance for us and for the whole world of that northern area, where there is not only an abundance of mineral resources of many kinds and a vast abundance of water power and other basic power, but also the fissionable materials from which undreamed of possibilities may emerge for those countries deficient in power, and because of that deficiency almost without hope of removing the poverty and distress which has been their lot for so long.
After a positive, clear and definite proposal for disarmament under international supervision and protection the President of the United States, speaking obviously not only on behalf of that country but also of Great Britain and France, proposed that there be set aside a great international pool or stockpile of fissionable materials for the continuing supply of such atomic and hydrogen weapons as might be necessary for the common defence of freedom, and also for the purpose of peaceful experiment and research, as a result of which fortunate lands like Canada and the United States might find new opportunities and other lands now in poverty might be offered resources of electrical power and agricultural advancement through the scientific employment of these minerals for peaceful purposes.
Surely a thought that will appeal to all mankind was the statement by the President this afternoon, made with unexcelled knowledge of the possibilities of its employment, that this most destructive of all forces, which today hangs as a cloud over the whole world, can become a boon greater than any that man has yet known. After proposing this
Canada Grain Act
international stockpile of normal uranium and fissionable material, he then challenged the imagination of his audience at the United Nations to contemplate what could be done if the scientists who are now devoting their energy to destruction used that accumulated knowledge in this new branch of science to explore the possibilities of the peaceful use of what he described as a bank of fissionable material for the production of electrical energy, which could be sent to the power-starved areas of the world, thus giving the nations which today see little sign of hope the possibilities of security, of happiness and of advancement which they could not foresee only a few years ago.
I find it difficult to believe that it is only a little more than 20 years ago that I flew to Great Bear lake and saw the new discovery of uranium at that distant point. At that time we thought simply of the possibilities of radium and of the scientific developments led by the Curies in Paris. It was on a later and tragic date in 1945 when the full menace of this new discovery dawned. Within those 20 years we have entered a new period in the history of the world.
If the offer extended so open-handedly today by the President of the United States at the United Nations, and so obviously with the support of Great Britain and France, is accepted in that spirit by the nations of the whole world-and I hope, as I believe we all hope, that it will be so accepted-then this northern area of Canada may become the centre of one of the greatest peaceful developments ever known to man.
Mr. Speaker, it is now five o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Canada Grain Act (distribution of box cars).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of once again proposing a new system for the distribution of box cars among elevator companies in western Canada. I believe the time is long since past when such a new method of box car distribution is necessary. Some may think, some may say, that the congestion now existing in western Canada in our grain marketing facilities is something of a very temporary nature, but I take issue with that point of

Canada Grain Act
view. I believe the congestion, we now have is likely to continue for some considerable time.
It used to be back in the 1930's, when grain crops were small, that elevators were often half empty or totally empty. And with a situation such as that you had real competition in the buying of grain. The farmer had a choice; he could take his grain to any elevator that he might wish to patronize, but the situation recently has been very much different. Elevators are almost always plugged. Farmers are short of money because they are not able to deliver a substantial quantity of grain. Therefore as soon as an elevator has some space available, farmers in that area feel obliged economically to haul grain to such elevator.
It used to be that elevator agents, like other business people, would obtain patrons if they had good business acumen I suppose you might term it, but such is not necessary now. The amount of business that is done by each elevator company at all of the points in western Canada is dependent almost solely on the number of box cars that are spotted at that company's elevator. The ability of the elevator agent does not matter so much. It does not matter too much whether farmers prefer that elevator company above others at that point. If the elevator company is given two box cars on a certain day, then the elevator agent will announce that he is prepared to buy 4,000 bushels of grain. Farmers will line up in front of that elevator the next day, and the grain will go into the elevator. When the 4,000 bushels have been marketed the sign will go up that no more grain can be accepted, and any farmers who have not been able to dump their loads will have to take them home. I say this is a situation that is not likely to be ended soon.
When I spoke in the debate a year ago on the same kind of bill I suggested to the minister that we might have a carryover at the end of July 31, 1953, of more than 330 million bushels of wheat. He said he did not believe those figures at all and called such a statement nonsense. But the actual carryover turned out to be 363 million bushels of wheat. Therefore I was a little too conservative in my estimate, but I was substantially correct. On the basis of the available quantities of wheat in the four exporting countries of the world today, in my judgment, we are going to face plugged elevators for another few years, at any rate. According to the wheat review for the month of October, on October 1, in the four exporting countries in the world, there were available for export and carryover 1,862 million bushels of wheat. That is sufficient wheat to All the international agreement as proposed before Britain withdrew.

It has been said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and others, "Oh, well, this situation comes about because we have had two or three abnormally large crops." They go on to say that if we get back to normal crops it will probably correct the situation. I think we are likely to continue for some time to get average crops or higher than average crops; and if I were to hazard a guess as to the size of the 1954 wheat crop I would say, on the basis of ample reserves of moisture on the three prairie provinces and bearing in mind that farmers are using better agricultural practices than ever before, that we are likely to obtain in 1954 an average or a better than average crop. If that should come about, then we are going to face once again the same kind of congestion we are facing at the present time.
Somebody of course distributes box cars among the elevator companies at all the marketing points. The way in which it is ordinarily done is to leave it in the hands of the local railway agent; to leave the distribution of box cars to the railway companies. Very often the railway agents take this attitude. If there are four elevator companies doing business at a certain marketing point, and eight cars come into that marketing point, they say that a fairly equitable system of distribution is to give each of the four elevator companies two box cars. They do not-and I do not think they should be asked to-attempt to assess whether the farmers in that locality want to deliver larger quantities of grain to one elevator company than to another. They just say, "Oh, well, this is a fairly equitable method; it is an easy method, and it is the one we shall follow."
The minister said last year his understanding was that the normal method was to give the pool elevator company twice as many box cars as any other elevator company. I doubt very much whether that kind of formula is followed at many points. If you had at a given elevator point just two or three companies involved and the wheat pool was given twice as many box cars as the other company, or as each of the other two companies, it would be a somewhat equitable method; but even that method, when followed at an elevator point that had six or seven or eight competing companies, would mean that the wheat pool system would be tied down to about 25 per cent or less of the box cars, and therefore it could not accept a quantity of grain in excess of 25 per cent of the grain hauled to that elevator point.
Someone may say all is well, we have a transport controller. We have, but the

transport controller himself would be the first to point out that he does not control the distribution of box cars among elevator companies at any of the marketing points in western Canada. In other words the transport controller is not in the business of box car distribution at all. The transport controller merely looks over the situation in western Canada, as I understand it, and if he sees a certain area that is getting fewer box cars than he thinks it is entitled to, he asks the railway companies to spot within that area a larger number of box cars. At what elevators the railway companies spot their box cars is the business of the elevator companies themselves.
There is another method of box car distribution that is used. It is a method that is provided for in the Canada Grain Act, and it is known as the car order book or the car order book system. Under that method a farmer may go into the railway station, direct the railway agent to produce the car order book, and order a car. Other farmers may come and each order a box car. This method was intended originally to protect the farmers against elevator companies that were taking excessive dockage or were underweighing; but it is now used instead to distribute box cars among the elevator companies. If one looks over the situation on the prairies it is very easy to see what elevator system is being discriminated against when box car distribution is left to the railway companies. You now have wheat pool farmers promoting the use of the car order book at as many marketing points as possible. Why?
Wheat pool officials have informed me that at almost every point where the car order book has been put into effect, wheat pool purchases have increased. So you have the wheat pool organization throughout western Canada promoting the use of the car order book system, a system which they would be the first to admit was not provided originally for that purpose. It is a clumsy system but it gets the pool more box cars.
It may lead to ill will when a certain farmer or group of farmers go into a railway station and order cars without notifying the community that they are putting the car order book system into effect. The larger farmers have an advantage because even with the small quotas in existence at the present time such a farmer may have sufficient grain to fill a box car. The smaller farmers must go together and order a box car collectively in order to market their grain.
The car order book system as we now have it is being used for purposes for which
Canada Grain Act
it was not intended. Because of that it is a clumsy and outdated method. The suggestion I make is not to dispose of the car order book provision, because the farmers of western Canada have come to regard the Canada Grain Act as their charter of rights and the car order book section as being an important provision. I would not want to interfere with the provisions of the car order book section, but I do ask the minister and the government to give consideration to a new and additional method which might be used for the spotting of box cars at any elevator point when the car order book system has not been put into effect.
My bill asks for a new section in the car order book provision so that when a farmer is filling in his permit book he might, before October 1 of any year, post his acreage among the elevator companies at that marketing point. For example, if a farmer had 300 acres of crop and there were three elevator companies doing business at that marketing point, he might want to deliver the product of 100 acres (to each of the three elevators. Or he might want to distribute 50 per cent of his acreage to one elevator and divide the remaining 50 per cent between the other two. Or he might want to post his entire acreage to one elevator company.
This new system would place once again in the hands of the producers the right to deliver grain to the elevator of their choice. They would assume the right to decide the proportion of box cars going to each elevator company. As I said at the outset, it does not matter now too much where the farmer wants to deliver his grain, as he is forced to deliver grain to the elevator company which has room. The elevator company which has room is the elevator company that is being given box cars.
I believe this provision is a sensible one. If the minister or the government believe that any improvement can be made in a principle such as this, I am not tied to the wording of this bill; but I do believe that such a provision, or a similar provision at any rate, is absolutely essential.
One of the things that has disturbed me is the practices that have been followed from time to time which I believe have resulted in a larger quantity of grain going through the line elevator companies than would otherwise be the case if the farmers had a method by which they could determine the distribution of box cars.
In July of this year quotas were removed completely, before the end of the crop year. I do not think my statement can be contradicted when I say that when those quotas

Canada Grain Act
were removed in July, the line companies throughout western Canada had a greater proportion of empty space than had the pool elevator systems. The quotas came off and the farmers were able to haul grain to any elevator at any point. It was by that method that the line elevators were filled.
On October 9 the car order book provision of the Canada Grain Act was arbitrarily discontinued by the transport controller. I am not saying there were not reasons for doing that, but one result was that further hundreds of thousands of bushels of grain were put through the line elevators. In support of that statement I have a letter from D. H. Munholland, secretary of the wheat pool at Strasbourg, Saskatchewan, dated December 1, 1953. It is addressed to my colleague the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher), and I would like to read two short paragraphs from the letter as follows:
When the transport controller discontinued the use of the car order book in October we were forced to accept 25 per cent of the box cars as there are four companies doing business on this market.
We have also records to prove that we have enjoyed 52 per cent of the grain receipts for the past 15 years.
In other words the pool elevator at that marketing point had 52 per cent of the business when the farmers were allowed to select their own elevator. Then the transport controller took away the car order book provision. The railroad companies then said, "We will not distribute box cars on the proportion of 52 per cent to the pool elevators where 52 per cent of the farmers want to do their business. We will give each of the four elevator companies 25 per cent of the box cars."
How would any hon. member of this house, particularly any member of the Conservative party, of the Liberal party or of the Social Credit party who professes to believe in free enterprise, like to be told that gasoline would be distributed in such a way that he must buy part of his gasoline requirements from a certain company? How would he like to be forced to buy a certain percentage of his repairs for his automobile from a certain company?
When cars were distributed at Strasbourg on the basis of 25 per cent to each elevator company you were forcing farmers at that point to market 75 per cent of their grain through the line elevators and 25 per cent through the pool elevator, even though 52 per cent of the grain under ordinary free competition would go through the pool elevator system.
