speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit a question? I hope he will appreciate that I am asking this question seriously, as I am seeking information on this point. When this matter was under debate on April 21, 1953, the then hon. member for The Battle-fords said, as will be found at page 4180 of Hansard:
I think I am correct in saying that at the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates last November or December a proposal similar to this was brought forward, and I think I am correct in saying it was voted down.
Could the hon. member give us detailed information on that subject?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
I think I could on that subject, but not on that specific question. I believe I stated at that time I would be extremely surprised if any such motion were defeated at the wheat pool convention in 1952. However, the wheat pool had its 1953 convention a few weeks ago, in the first part of November. I am coming to that at a later point, but let me tell my hon. friend right now that a resolution was passed at the annual wheat pool convention held in Regina early in November asking for a new system of box car distribution along the lines I have outlined in my bill. Naturally, in a resolution they could not set out a bill, but I shall quote to the house the exact wording of that resolution; and I can also report from conversations I have had with officials of pool elevators that they would support the principle of the bill that I am moving this afternoon.
I do not say they would not want their law officers to go over it and perhaps make minor amendments, but certainly they would support the provision that farmers be allowed to post their acreage among elevator companies thereby deciding the percentage of box cars that shall go to each elevator. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the action that has been taken by the wheat board in removing quotas and by the transport controller in cancelling the car order book has resulted in the line elevator system being given additional millions of bushels of grain when, if the western farmers had a free choice, these line elevator companies might never have received any of it.
I am hopeful the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who believes in free competition and certainly I think should believe in giving people freedom of choice, should restore some competition in the buying of grain in western Canada, since that competition, because of congestion, is largely non-existent at the present time.

I have a letter from Mr. Peter Eppon, secretary of the Wilkie, Saskatchewan, wheat pool committee in western Canada. This well-documented letter contains a wealth of information, but I shall read only the last two or three points from his letter to me. He states that on May 5, 1953, when the quota was raised at Wilkie from 8 bushels to 15 bushels per acre, the space distribution was as follows: In the pool elevator there was space for only 5,893 bushels of grain, and in the other two line elevator companies there was space for 52,900 bushels.
In other words, there was over eight times the space in the other two elevators as compared with that available in the pool elevator, when the quota was raised. On May 6, 1953, Mr. Eppon said the quota was raised at Wilkie from 15 to 18 bushels per acre and the space distribution was as follows: The space available at the pool elevator was 4,992 bushels, whereas the space available at the other two elevators was 57,900, or a ratio of 11 to 1. Once again the quota was such that these other elevator companies would soon have their space filled. On July 21, when the quota was taken off, there was space at the pool elevator for 9,429 bushels, and at the other two elevators for 74,500 bushels.
I repeat the result of the policy now followed, and as outlined in the letters I have read to the house, is to force farmers to market a large percentage of their grain through the line elevator system. I must point out that the adoption of the bill could and no doubt would at some elevator points in western Canada result in the line elevator agent receiving a higher proportion of box cars and a larger proportion of grain because some line elevator agents are very popular persons. They may be at what is ordinarily a weak pool elevator point, and if farmers were given a free choice in box car distribution it is more than likely that at a large number of points the line elevators would buy a larger proportion of grain than the pool.
Fine and good; I would not object to that at all. I would like to see it happen, because what I want to see happen is the producers having the right to market grain at elevators of their own choice, but until they have control of box car distribution that cannot happen.
When I spoke in this debate last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce had some objections which I do not think were particularly valid. The minister said that to bring in provisions such as I have included in Bill No. 3 would mean a great rigidity in the distribution of box cars. Supposing,
Canada Grain Act
he asked, an elevator has a lot of spoiled grain? That elevator company, he asserted, would need quite a substantial number of box cars in order to move out the grain that might be in danger of spoiling.
I would be quite happy to see, as I probably would in any case, section 68, paragraph 2, of the Canada Grain Act applied to this provision as it now applies to the car order book, which gives the board of grain commissioners the right to send in more box cars in order to prevent grain from spoiling. I would go so far as to say that I would not object to this formula not being followed for a substantial period of time if there were valid reasons just so long as each company had received its percentage of box cars at the year's end. I would not care if I knew that my pool elevator on this formula was to get 60 per cent of the box cars and the line elevators got 20 per cent each. If the line elevator got 20 one day and the pool got none it would make no difference as long as over the period of a year box cars would be provided up to 60 per cent to the pool and 40 per cent for the line elevators, as determined by the producers.

rigid that the transport controller from time to time has suspended the provisions of the car order book. I say that if this formula were placed in the Canada Grain Act it would be much less rigid than the present system and would serve a very useful purpose.
I will read the provisions I have suggested. My bill provides that the Canada Grain Act is amended by inserting therein immediately after section 72 the following sections:
72A. Any producer, as defined in section 15 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, chapter 44 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, may, before the first day of October in any year, enter in the car order book his acreage seeded to grain as shown in his permit book pursuant to sections 18 and 19 of the said act, and may assign that acreage among the elevator companies at his marketing point.
72B. If-

Section 72B reads as follows:
If, at any time, no unfilled application for a car appears in the car order book at a marketing point, the railway agent shall then apportion railway cars among the elevator companies in the proportion that the acreage has been divided among the elevator companies.
I say that provision is a whole lot less rigid than listing 100 farmers under the car order book system and having to spot in rotation at a certain elevator, as specified in the car order book, each individual car as it comes in. We have a rigid formula now. The trouble is that when it is removed the producer has no control. As was done in the case to which I referred, the railway agent can say that each elevator shall get

25 per cent of the box cars. That is a rigid formula. The elevator agent can spot the box cars as he sees fit.
This is another thing that happens. Everybody is human. We all like to have friends, and some people are better friends of ours than others. You have the human element, and I know it is true there are instances of definite favouritism shown by railway officials when they themselves, not the transport controller, have the right as they now have to distribute box cars when the car order book system is not in effect.
I come to the question asked by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) with respect to where the farm organizations, and particularly the wheat pool, stand with regard to this matter. In the Western Producer of November 19, which is the wheat pool publication, there appears an article headed "Seek Changes in Grain Act". The article goes on to say that a committee composed of officials from the three prairie pools was set up last year, that a submission was brought in and that certain recommendations were agreed to. The article continues:
In the directors' report to the delegates, the board recommended an effort be made to find a workable plan for the equitable distribution of cars between elevators and shipping points throughout the three provinces on the basis of the amount of grain handled-
That is on the basis of past experience. If the pool elevators handled 52 per cent of the grain in the last 15 years they would want 52 per cent of the box cars. I continue: -or to be handled during the season, to the end that growers may be able to deliver grain to the country elevator of their choice.
I say my bill is perfectly in keeping with that recommendation, which asks for a new provision for the spotting of box cars in such a way as to enable farmers to deliver grain to the elevator of their own choice. We have the wheat board system of marketing grain, which the producers support. We have a quota system established from time to time, which the producers support. We have the Canada Grain Act with certain provisions in it for a car order book, but from time to time somebody comes along and interferes with the quota system and removes it altogether, or interferes with the operation of the Canada Grain Act by cancelling the car order book.
Then you are faced with the situation we now have, where farmers, because of economic necessity, are forced to market their grain at elevators where they would not otherwise market it.

I believe this problem can be solved. The transport controller has said that he is not in a position to solve it, and he will not try to do so. But the wheat pool officials in western Canada have definite recommendations as to how the problem can be solved.

Let me say to the minister that I have talked with officials of the pool elevator system, I have talked with delegates, I have talked with directors of the pool organization, and from the statements made to me I can say they feel that a bill along the lines of the one I am presenting is workable and is in the interests of the producers of western Canada.
I say to the minister that there is a better method for the distribution of box cars than either letting the railway companies do it, which is what prevails in most instances now, or the car order book system which the pool officials have said is out of date. I suggest that by allowing the farmers to post their acreage and decide what percentage of box cars shall be spotted at the various elevator companies at the different points in western Canada you would have a method that is not nearly as cumbersome and rigid as the present car order book system, and a method similar to the one now followed in the distribution of box cars by railway agents with the great difference that whereas the railway companies now decide the percentage of box cars spotted at each elevator this bill would enable the producers to determine the distribution of box cars.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
I feel, Mr. Speaker, I should say a word on this bill at this stage. To begin with, I do not agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat on the point he has been trying to make for the last forty minutes, that the distribution of box cars throughout western Canada
Canada Grain Act
has been most inequitable. So far as I could ascertain throughout the country I think it is fair to say, and I think it should be said in fairness to the railways and the officials of the Canadian wheat board concerned in this business, that a sincere effort has been made to distribute the box cars as equitably as possible under all the circumstances. I know that in my home town and many other centres throughout the country I never heard anyone complain that the distribution of the box cars was made in the inequitable way that has been mentioned this afternoon.
This does not mean, of course, that there is no criticism of the system as a whole. We have been going through a period when the box car situation has been very tight. There have not been enough box cars to go around at each point, and as long as this situation continues there will be some people who will be dissatisfied at not getting as many box cars as they want. My impression is that the criticism is of the distribution of box cars as between areas or between provinces. Of course that is a different question than the one which is dealt with in this bill. So far as the distribution locally in a given centre is concerned, I want to repeat that the distribution has been done as fairly as was humanly possible in view of the shortage of box cars and the shortage of space.
The hon. member tried to make quite a point out of the free choice by the producers between elevators and box cars. This is a very laudable objective and what everybody is working toward, but so long as box cars are not available it will be very difficult to achieve that objective. He argued that the alternative to this was the car order book. This is not the first time the hon. member has used strong words in complaining about the arbitrary way in which the controller suspended the operation of the car order book. Yet in the same breath the hon. member made it quite clear that he did not believe the car order book was a good system to follow.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext: Not at all; I did not say that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
That was the impression I got. If the hon. member believes in the car order book system, why would he request an alternative to that system? I think it should be said that the car order book system has not been removed from the act, as was stated by several members in this house in a previous debate. This provision is still a part of the Canada Grain Act, and I believe it should remain a part of the Canada Grain Act. I believe the principle is a good one. Whenever we reach the stage where the controller says the number of box cars is sufficient, then
718

Canada Grain Act
by all means the producer should have the right of choice. If the producer is not satisfied with the line elevator company, then he should have the right to load his grain in box cars. So long as these box cars are not available, I would go so far as to say that I doubt very much if the car order book system could be operated successfully or even equitably.
When the controller was appointed a few years ago, as all hon. members know, we had one of the most difficult situations we have had at any time. One of the first things the controller did was to suspend the car order book. There has been quite a demand from various quarters to have the car order book reinstated. I understand that this system will be reinstated on the 14th of this month. Although I agree with the principle of the car order book system, I have some doubt that this procedure should be followed so long as there is a shortage of cars and a shortage of space. My opinion is that when the system is reinstated there will be an abuse of it, and it will have to be suspended again in the near future.
What the hon. member is trying to do is suggest a method of replacing the car order book, but if we proceed on the basis that the car order book has not flexibility and cannot be successfully operated during a period when cars are short, such as we have now, then his argument fails. Apparently this bill would put into the Canada Grain Act loading measures that would have the same practical effect as the car order book. I might say in passing that the hon. member is trying to get the support of the house for the principle of this bill, if not for the bill itself. Of course we are considering second reading of the bill, and we have no choice but to support the principle and not the bill. We have no alternative at this time.
In considering this bill we must consider the exact wording of it, and how it will affect the Canada Grain Act. I think that rather than amend the Canada Grain Act by inserting a provision which is so fluid and so uncertain, we should leave the field open for the controller and give some leeway, especially in view of the experience we have had with the car order book. If a system could be devised that would give the producer a free choice to go to any elevator, then it would presuppose that there are sufficient cars and sufficient space.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) more or less left the impression that he was quite disturbed that such large quantities of grain were delivered to the elevators. He made a point of saying that the elevator companies benefited greatly from this. Of course at the time the idea was to give the

farmers an opportunity of delivering their grain in order to realize cash. They tried to get all the space they could and fill it with grain.
Naturally that enabled a lot of farmers to deliver grain and realize some money on it. That is the very complaint at this moment, the complaint connected with surpluses on the western farms. What we want to do is get the grain away from the farms so we will still realize money on it. Surely hon. members should not critieize the board when it takes the grain and stores it, and at the same time criticize it for not taking the grain out on the farms. Hon. members cannot have it both ways. Certainly the board made an honest effort at that time. In criticizing what it does, hon. members should try at least to be helpful in their criticism.

speechtext: Does the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) know whether or not the Canadian wheat board, when it lifted the quotas on July 21, consulted farm organizations in western Canada? If so, did any farm organization .recommend the removal of all quotas.

speechtext:
Of course I know very well the quota was opened last summer. As to whether or not the wheat board consulted the farm organizations, one must keep in mind that after all the handling of grain by the board is no small business, no small responsibility. Surely it would be too much to expect the wheat board, at every move they make, to hold conferences and consultations for a week before taking action. I do not know whether the time element permitted them to have such consultations, or whether they were in a position to consult. It may be that they had phone calls; they might have phoned two or three people in the farm movement group, but this would not appear on the files. For all I know they might have held consultations.
The point I make is that their action was certainly an earnest effort to try to relieve the situation. This is not the first time that my hon. friend and some of his followers in the socialist group have advanced criticism of this type. I well recall that when an advance payment was made a few years ago there was an outcry from the socialist group to the effect that the advance payment should not have been made. That action was followed by a very persistent attempt by all groups in the opposition to have an advance payment made. Then the moment it was made there was an insinuation that it had been made for political purposes, and all that sort of thing.
Well, time has proved that this has been done year in and year out, in election years

and in years when there have been no elections. Yet the fact that it was made that year prompted criticism from certain quarters, and my hon. friend was one who joined in that criticism.

speechtext: That was an interim payment.

speechtext:
Yes, it was an interim payment, an advance interim payment. This year the crop year is extended for a little while, and we have another situation. I do not know if the board has consulted every organization, but it is very conceivable that the time element would not allow the officials of the board to hold conferences with various groups. Then again we have heard the cry that this was done because it was an election year. Well, probably it was an election year; but surely we had no control over the rain, even if we did control certain things in the election.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

Yes, and the people had the final control of it; my hon. friend should know that. As a matter of fact the very members who levelled that criticism against the interim payment have stayed home from this parliament, with probably the one exception of a member who went to an urban seat to get elected.
Then I come to the next subject, that of farm storage. I shall not deal with it because there is another bill on that subject.
In conclusion let me say that in my humble opinion since this measure is designed in effect to replace the car order book, I do not believe it would help the problem in any way, shape or form. Indeed, there is a great possibility that it may make the condition worse. I do not suppose anyone would quarrel with the general principle of the bill, that of trying to obtain fair and equitable distribution. From my own personal experience, however, I would say that I know of no railway agent who has shown what my hon. friend has described as favouritism. All the ones I have known have tried to do the best they could in the circumstances, and they have done pretty well.
The railways have tried to distribute their box cars. Unfortunately, however, in the last two years, for one reason or another, I know in my own district the Canadian
Northern Affairs and National Resources Pacific Railway has to some extent fallen down on the job. I am sure they would have a very good explanation for having done so, but the fact remains that box cars have not been forthcoming from the C.P.R. to the same extent that they have been available from the Canadian National Railways, despite the fact that the two railways are close to each other. At one point only a few miles separate the two lines. Apparently they were committed beforehand last year, but I was surprised when they found themselves in the same predicament this year.
All in all, however, they have tried to make a fair allocation and have done their best to meet the situation. I think the answer should be left to the controller himself. Possibly he could look into the matter even more closely.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there has been ample indication of the general support of the measure before the house to leave no doubt that anything that may be said is simply to emphasize the belief of hon. members who speak that in all our minds there is a firm conviction that great days lie ahead in the development of the northland of this country of ours.
In presenting the bill now before us the Prime Minister gave some figures which indicate the vastness of the area that will be affected by that part of the activities of the department that is directed mainly to our northland. It is a challenging thought to realize that today we live in the third largest country in the world, and the largest country in the free world at this time. It is also a challenging thought to realize that
718	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources such a large part of the 3,800,000 and more square miles that make up the area of Canada lies in the distant north.
There was a time when well-informed writers could speak of Canada as a whole as a land of ice and snow. Today, throughout the whole modern world the eyes and the thoughts and the hopes of many people are turned toward this country. Even yet many of us living in Canada are inclined to have that same thought of that vast northland. Nothing will ever change the fact that the true north, the far north, is bound to be a land of ice and snow for a considerable part of the year, but it can also be a land of great beauty and great attractiveness. It is a land of great opportunity, a land that beckons to the able and the vigorous and to people of all ages who still seek adventure and are prepared to put effort into that adventure which pays great rewards.
It is still difficult for us to visualize the distances that separate some parts of that great northland from our centres of population. Only in these past few days we have been learning of the plans that are being made for the removal of Aklavik and Coppermine on the Arctic coast to more secure sites. It does arouse the imagination of every Canadian to think that the distance from Edmonton, which we sometimes regard as one of our northern cities, to Aklavik is something over 1,200 miles straight north. That is not an area barren of opportunity, no matter how barren it may be in appearance.
I spoke for a moment this afternoon of being on the shores of Great Bear lake more than twenty years ago, just after the discovery of the first uranium mine in this country. At that same time I visited different parts of the Arctic coast during the brief period of the year which has twenty-four hours of daylight, and I can scarcely recall having seen more beautiful or more vivid flowers anywhere in Canada than I saw along the Arctic coast around the settled communities from Aklavik to Coppermine. It is a rugged country. It is a country that is certainly not meant for those who expect any easy return for their efforts, but it is a country that offers many possibilities to us and to future generations, with the modern devices which have now become available and have changed the whole way of life in that distant land.
As we now join in emphasizing our faith in the future of the Canadian north, in expressing our support for this measure, we might well recall those gallant young men who had so much to do with this new day that has


dawned in that great northland. There is no more romantic story in Canadian history, or perhaps in the history of any country, than the story of those young bush pilots who more than twenty years ago were carrying tremendous loads of freight into the uncharted settlements of the north, who were making possible those discoveries which have meant so much to us within these past few years and are going to mean so much to us in the years ahead. They carried every conceivable kind of supply that could be freighted. They carried machinery; they carried fuel; they carried the needs of those who were exploring for mining properties at that time.
It is a great story of courage, of achievement and of adventure, one that every young Canadian should know. Now that airfields, organized air routes and highways have been built right through to Alaska it is a very different picture. Most of us, perhaps all of us, will join with the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Simmons) in the hope that a road may be completed from Dawson that will connect with the Alaska highway and bring direct communication to that extremely encouraging part of our great northland.
I do raise one question in regard to this measure. I do so with the hope that it may be given consideration. I certainly have no intention of moving an amendment to the bill, because it is starting a department, which already exists substantially in the same form, on a new course, with greater emphasis on northern development. I should like to refer only to the fact that one of the subjects that is referred to this department and placed under its control is Eskimo affairs. Already the suggestion has been made that it is natural to place Eskimo affairs under one department and Indian affairs under another. I do not know whether I can entirely agree with that suggestion, although I appreciate the reasons that support it.
If there is one aspect of our collective responsibility as a society which should give us no feeling of satisfaction it is the plight today of more than 100,000 Indians in this country. No matter what the explanations may be, no matter how we may explain the position of the Indians under the ancient treaties which gave them their special position and certain protection and certain rights, I do not see how any person who believes in equality within this democracy of ours can be satisfied with the status of the Indians of this country at this time.
We have not succeeded in giving them the kind of equality that we say should be extended to people in other countries. I am

Northern Affairs and National Resources
not prepared to agree that there is any inherent weakness in the Indians that makes them incapable of development by proper education if that education is extended to them at the right time. I have seen the results of education among the Indians where that education was accorded in early childhood. I recall a most interesting experiment with which I had some association as minister of education in Ontario when we opened a modern, well-equipped school on the shore of James bay. There young Indians have been receiving the same kind of education as other children in Ontario, and the results demonstrate that a young Indian, given the same opportunity, even at a point in the fairly distant north, can absorb that education and benefit from it.
I realize all the difficulties presented by this problem. I realize that many of the Indians themselves feel that there is a certain measure of protection under these ancient treaties which they would not lightly abandon. To them their tribal customs are cherished traditions. Nevertheless we cannot be satisfied until in some way we have found a method by which every young Indian, wherever that is possible, is given a chance to obtain at least a satisfactory elementary education.
Having said that, I wish now to return to Eskimo affairs. There are a number of hon. members who have seen the Eskimos along the Arctic coast and elsewhere. Those who have will agree that they have never seen such a naturally happy people anywhere at any time. That is the most distinguishing characteristic of the Eskimo. They seem to find something to laugh or to smile about in every event of their very stern life. They are brave, they are courageous, they are energetic; they are a most attractive people.
We are not hampered in the plans that may be made for their advancement by any of these ancient arrangements which in some measure cannot be disregarded and under which the government of course must recognize its obligations. However, it does not seem to me that the reason is too clear why these two problems should be separated. Granted, a very large part of our Indian population is in the southern part of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. On the other hand, a considerable part of the population where the greatest problems arise in according equality of citizenship is in the northland where nomadic Indian tribes move about and present increasing difficulties by their very movement.
However, these people do come in contact with the Eskimo. As you travel through the Northwest Territories you pass from the land
occupied by the Indians immediately into the land occupied by the Eskimos. In years gone by they used to constantly fight each other. One of the famous spots on the Coppermine river running north into the Arctic is a place known as Bloody Falls near the town of Coppermine where a tremendous battle was fought years ago between the Eskimos and the Indian Dogrib tribe occupying that area.
Historic spots of that kind simply serve to emphasize that there are differences, that there are reasons for dealing with this subject in a way that recognizes the basic differences in the problem itself. Nevertheless it does seem to me that consideration might be given to the advantages that would be gained by bringing Indian affairs and Eskimo affairs together in the same department so that health experts, experts in the educational field and others, finding reasons to go into the northland to visit the Indians, could extend their" trips only a short distance further and visit the Eskimos. That would seem a reasonable economy of effort. It would seem also to suggest the possibilities of finding ideas that might be helpful in dealing with the affairs of these two native groups of people within our country.
I have indicated on many occasions in this house my own faith in the opportunities of the north; I hope that in some measure I demonstrated that faith on earlier occasions when I had some responsibility in regard to what we called the north, but which is really the south when we examine the great map of Canada.
Events of the past few years; new types of vehicles; the possibility of electric power; transportable diesel power, and certainly the development of uranium and fissionable energy which we are assured can become a reality in the near future, are things that call for the imagination, vision and faith of a people who have seen great developments take place but who live in a country which in terms of history is still very young. As we express our faith-we have every reason to repeat it over and over again-in Canada we have every reason to also express our faith in the great future of the northland which has been under discussion today.
I should like to think of the appeal to our imagination that came years ago in the poems of Robert W. Service, which made the distant north a land of romance to many of us. But Robert W. Service never left any doubt that it was a land that would be developed only by the hardy, the strong and the bold,
720	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources and I am sure most members here, probably all, will remember those opening lines of the "Song of the Yukon":
This is the law ol the Yukon,
And ever she makes it plain:
Send not your foolish and feeble;
Send me your strong and your sane.
That was the beginning of a poem that pictured the challenge of the north and the great possibilities of the north which Robert W. Service saw so clearly so many years ago.
These lines I have just read apply with equal force to all that great north with its rewards in return for the effort that is made in building for the future. It can support a great population. It can make a great contribution to the future of Canada, and I am sure all of us agree with what has already been said about the advantage of extending more and more and as rapidly as possible a form of self-government comparable to that now shared by the provinces of that country. I am sure there will be members of this house, particularly the younger members who are with us now, who will see the time when a new province of Canada will emerge in that great northland.
It offers a challenge to every young Canadian, and I for one support this measure with the greatest enthusiasm in the hope that it will not merely be a change in the name of a department, but that with the introduction of this measure and with the aid of the minister who will guide its affairs every Canadian will be reminded that such a large part of this country still remains to be developed, and that the future of Canada will very largely be measured by what we do in the north.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Mackenzie constituency extends to the Northwest Territories I would like to make some comment on the bill before the house, but before proceeding I would like to comment very briefly on the outstanding statement made at the United Nations this afternoon by President Eisenhower. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) pointed out before dinner, this statement would indicate that this new department may become one of the very important departments of the Canadian government. I quote from this afternoon's press:
President Eisenhower called today on the world's atomic powers to reverse "the fearful trend" of the atomic arms race and to set up under the United Nations an international atomic energy agency to develop the peaceful potential of the atom. In a dramatic speech made against the [Mr. Drew.l

background of the Bermuda conference, the President declared "the Soviet union must, of course, be one" of the nations participating in any such project.
Then the President put forth these proposals:
First-Encourage world-wide investigation into the most effective peacetime uses of fissionable material;
Second-Begin to diminish the potential destructive power of the world's atomic stockpiles;
Third-Allow all peoples of all nations to see that, in this enlightened age, the great powers of the earth, those of the east and the west, are interested in human aspirations, first and foremost, rather than in building up the armaments of war;
Fourth-Open up a new channel for peaceful discussion and initiate at least a new approach to the many difficult problems that must be solved in both public and private conferences if the world is to shake off the inertia imposed by fear and make positive progress toward peace.
I believe, though I have not any information to support it, that Sir Winston Churchill should receive some credit for this important statement. When I was in London in October there was a good deal of gossip there to the effect that Sir Winston was more concerned about being remembered as helpful in saving the peace than he was in playing the important role that he did play during the second world war, and it had been suggested by his friends that he should go to the United Nations and make the sort of speech that President Eisenhower made this afternoon.
This suggestion apparently was not accepted but I feel that the discussions at the Bermuda conference will give people all over the world hope and confidence in our ability to resolve our differences peacefully. I think this statement made by the President should add some weight to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) this afternoon that consideration should be given in Canada to setting up an authority similar to the TVA in the United States. With the great resources we have in the north country and the part uranium is likely to play in the future, I think favourable consideration should be given to this sort of proposal.
The dominion government already has a very large investment in the Eldorado Mining and Refining corporation, and I am sure much larger investments are going to be made in future. Like other members who have spoken in this debate I am very enthusiastic about the possibilities of the north country. The Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company has its offices in Manitoba, but the largest part of their underground operations are carried on in the province of Saskatchewan. The boundary between the two provinces runs right through this rich deposit. While we hear a great deal about:

the part free enterprise has played in the development of the country, and I would like to give credit to the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company, I think we should not lose sight of the fact that all of the people in Canada have a part in any great development.
When the ore was discovered a number of years ago it was recognized immediately as a very rich ore being composed of 3-2 per cent copper, 4-0 per cent zinc, 1-06 per cent silver and 0-075 ounces of gold. When this ore wTas discovered there was no known process that would enable any mining corporation in Canada or the United States to separate these valuable deposits, and it was here in Ottawa in the old department of mines and resources that civil servants worked out a process that later made it possible for the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company to proceed with this very large development. When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pleads on behalf of the retired civil servants I think we should remember that civil servants never stake a claim, are never able to invest large amounts in gold or uranium, but carry on a day to day work that must be done; and in doing this they discovered how copper, zinc, silver and gold could be separated.
I think the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company has as good a record as any large corporation in Canada. The fact that the provincial boundary runs right through their operations creates some border incidents from time to time. In Saskatchewan the workmen's compensation benefits are a good deal more attractive than in Manitoba. One story relates that a man started up a ladder which had its base in Manitoba and the top in Saskatchewan. He fell and landed partly in Manitoba and partly in Saskatchewan. His friends came to his rescue and brought him across the line, and he was therefore in Saskatchewan when the case was reported. On the whole, though, we are able to resolve these differences without any serious difficulty.
A subsidiary of this company, the Churchill River Power Company, Limited, has its operation entirely in Saskatchewan on the Churchill river. Island Falls is a company town, but if all company towns were like it I am sure there would not be too many criticisms levelled. Since I first started going to Island Falls some twelve or thirteen years ago all the old log houses have been replaced by attractive modern houses. I imagine they would cost from $12,000 to $15,000 if built in Ottawa. They are all electrically heated, and all have electric lights, frigidaires and electric ranges. The only two chimneys in
Northern Affairs and National Resources the town are for the fireplaces in the homes of the superintendent and the assistant superintendent. The schools are very well equipped. The teachers are paid higher salaries than teachers in the cities in the province, and the people who live at Island Falls have what would be considered a very high standard of living.
But as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) suggested, conditions for the Indian people living nearby are very different. The Indian village over at Sandy Bay is quite a different world, but I do not propose to discuss that tonight. However, I say that when the white man brings liquor to these Indian communities, and brings the knowhow for the making of illicit liquor, the rest of us have some responsibility for the very demoralizing influences that liquor has in these Indian communities.
Farther north in Saskatchewan, of course, we have these rich uranium deposits, and according to the information in the publication, "Saskatchewan, Its Resources and Industries", Saskatchewan uranium promises to place Canada on a par with the Belgian Congo as a source of atomic fuel.
There is one important section in the bill that has not been mentioned yet, that having to do with historic sites and monuments. While I think it is very important that we look to the future, we should not forget the past; and I am very glad the minister is to have this responsibility because I feel that with his imagination and energy he will give our historic places and monuments the attention that they deserve. When I travel over the northern part of my constituency by air with all the ease and pleasure of modem travel, I never forget that two and three hundred years ago people travelled through that country by very different methods.
I suggest to hon. members that they have a look at Kelsey's Papers which are available in the library. In 1689 Kelsey travelled over the northern part of my constituency when the going was very different. On the 2nd of July he made this note:
The same going as before at noon it raind hard having no shelter but y heavens for a cannope nor no wood to make a fire came dist twelve miles.
Of course there were other days when things were a little rosier. On the 28th of August he had good luck with geese, because his note reads;
Today about noon I went home w y Indian y came last night & carryed w us 19 geese.
That was quite a red letter day for Kelsey, because the whole of his travels from Hudson bay down as far as Touchwood on the plains was apparently a series of hardships. For
722	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources a number of years the national parks and historic sites service have had a good deal of trouble in getting enough money from governments of all complexions to do a worth-while job. I have had a report on the Fort Pelly situation. I have a letter from Colonel Childe, superintendent of the historic parks and sites branch, written on the 27th November, 1953. I am sure the material will be of interest to hon. members. He says:
Some thirty years ago we had considerable correspondence with the Hudson's Bay Company regarding the five acre plot on which the remains of Fort Pelly then stood. The company offered to sell this property to the department for the sum of $1,125-
When one considers the price the Hudson's Bay Company paid for the millions of acres they got it is pretty hard to understand why they put a price of $1,125 on the five acres representing the old site of Fort Pelly. I continue:
-later reduced to $750, and finally to $500, but the historic sites and monuments board of Canada decided that the latter figure was still too high, and the matter was dropped. This five acre plot was acquired later by the Pelly ladies homemakers club.
You will remember that you brought to the attention of the then deputy minister of mines and resources in August, 1949, a letter you had received from Mr. Lome M. Brandon, stating that the Pelly ladies homemakers club had decided to sell this property back to the original owner, as a result of which the matter was referred to the historic sites and monuments board at its meeting in 1950. The board deferred action to its 1951 meeting, in order to enable the Saskatchewan representative, Mr. Gregory, to make further investigation. Unfortunately, Mr. Gregory was forced by ill health to resign from the board, and his successor, Mr. Campbell Innes, who had just been appointed, was not in a position at the 1951 meeting to make a report, so the matter was again deferred. At its 1952 meeting the board again deferred its recommendation for further study, but in June, 1952, we were advised that the recently formed Fort Pelly historical society had purchased this five acre plot and offered it free to the government of Canada as a national historic site.
At its meeting in May, 1953, the board declared the site of Fort Pelly to be of national historic importance and recommended that the department accept the gift of the five acre plot of land on which the fort stood. Subsequently, we requested the surveyor general to arrange for a survey and to supply a copy of the survey plan and legal description of the site.
I am very happy to see that this transaction has been completed. I should mention that up in that area they have a very active historical society, and I am sure the minister will be interested in knowing that a paper like the Canora Courier, for example, carried three important articles of special historic interest in its issue of November 19. One is a letter from Fort Ellice to Fort Pelly written in 1864 by a W. McKay. Another is a report
IMr. Nicholson.]

of the annual meeting of the Fort Pelly historical society which contains the following:
With its membership of 93, the society is the largest historical society in Saskatchewan, said President Wylie in his opening remarks.
As I said, I think hon. members should be interested in the fact that at a time when the Hudson's Bay Company, which really should have been interested in having this spot developed as a historic site, was holding out for $1,125, then $750, and finally $500, we had a group of public-spirited citizens who on their own account raised money to buy the property so they could make a gift of it to the crown, and I say we should at least be able to find some funds to help to restore this old establishment. I hope the minister will accept an invitation from me at this point to visit the Fort Pelly historical society when he is making his tour across Canada in connection with his duties, so that he may be able to see some of the most interesting places in that area.
Another story in the newspaper to which I have referred tells about mine detectors being used in the Fort Pelly area with the result that two sites were located where posts are said to have been built. The article reads in part as follows:
Marlboro house was built in 1793 and old records show that Belleau's outpost was in existence during the trading season 1795-6.
My forebears went up to Queen's Bush in Bruce county about one hundred years ago.
I should like hon. members to recall that in the new north years before, between 1793 and 1795, there was a great deal of activity. Quite near Fort Pelly is found Fort Livingstone. The federal government, I am happy to say, has erected a plaque there which says:
Fort Livingstone First Capital of the
North-West Territories.
Here Lieutenant Governor Laird and his Council were sworn into office ' on 27th November, 1876, and here, on 8th March, 1877, was held the first session of the North-West Council.
Mrs. Gertrude S. Telford, now of Regina, did an interesting study for McMaster University when she was living in Pelly some years ago. She has this to say about Fort Livingstone:
In 1873 the site of Fort Livingstone (named for the great missionary who died that year) was chosen as the seat of government for the Northwest Territories and as headquarters for the newly-formed North-West Mounted Police.
In 1874 the contract for buildings was let to Hugh Sutherland who, with a gang of eighty to

one hundred men, began work on the site selected, September 1874. October 21 the same year the police arrived under the command of Colonel French who was dismayed to see the nature of the site chosen.
Apparently even in those days the people who were responsible made mistakes in selecting sites. Colonel French wrote in his diary as follows:
To my horror I found the barracks in course of construction on the top of a hill covered with large granite boulders, no trees to protect the buildings and these latter strung out in a line of a thousand feet long, exposing a full broadside to the north, the ground burned up to within 20 feet of the barracks. Still worse half the hay cut had been burned, the Hudson's Bay Company from whom we might have purchased losing 300 loads.
General Steele described the place as follows:
The Swan river barracks (Fort Livingstone) were built on a most extraordinary spot. How on earth any person in his senses could have selected it is difficult to imagine. The surface of the ground was covered with boulders and before space could be cleared to enable the men to form properly on parade we had to build large fires over the rocks and then pour water over them when hot to split them. Moreover the place was alive with snakes which were sometimes found even in the barrack rooms.
I suggest that before the minister visits the site of Fort Livingstone he should get a model A Ford, if possible, because the road is a hazardous one. There are so many good sites in the area it is difficult to imagine why this particular site was chosen. It may have been a good place for horses, but it is quite hazardous for one travelling in a modern car. I hope the new department will be able to find ways and means of making it possible to get into the old site safely because it is a lovely location overlooking the Swan river.
In conclusion may I say that I am sure the minister, who has many years of service ahead, will be bringing imagination to this important post. I am happy that he has agreed to meet the Saskatchewan minister of highways on the 15th to discuss the important question of building roads in the north. I think it is quite obvious that, in view of the potential wealth in the north, federal funds should be made available for road construction in that area.
I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) has been able to make an arrangement with the Saskatchewan government for fuller cooperation. Shortly before this session opened I was in the school at Pelican Narrows where a new arrangement is being worked out for the first time. There I saw the children of treaty Indians, metis, and white children studying together in a two-room school. The minister, as the one in charge of the Indians,
Northern Affairs and National Resources signed an agreement with the Saskatchewan minister of education to provide joint-educational services	to make	this experimentpossible. I am	sure	that	what has	been
achieved in the field of education can be achieved in other fields.
I express the hope that the minister will live to see this become one of the very important departments of government, with ample resources available to embark on a program such as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) suggested this afternoon when he	said	that	we might	have
publicly-owned utilities to harness the great resources of the north.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with very great interest to what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had to say this afternoon. I was particularly interested in hearing him say that the bill now before us	not	only	provides a	new
name for the present Department of Resources and Development, but it also indicates a shift in emphasis. I believe he said also that with the introduction of this bill he was indicating to the people of Canada that the centre of gravity in the department concerned is being moved north.
Now, because of that shift in emphasis and the fact that the centre of gravity of the department is being shifted to the north, those of us whose constituencies border on that great northland are perhaps a bit more interested in what is going to happen than those who are living farther away. I would judge that those of us who come from constituencies in the far north will have ideas to express to the Prime Minister and to the minister of the new department in the course of this debate tonight.
While it is quite clear, I think, that the great northland is a land of tremendous wealth my experience with it-and I have been travelling into the north country for about seventeen or eighteen years-would indicate that the resources are many in variety. They are resources that need developing. When they are developed they will contribute greatly to the strength of Canada as a whole. I am hoping also that they will receive the kind of development which will promote the well-being of the people who live in the area, as well as the people of Canada as whole. Of course that will depend on the manner in which they are developed.
I am directing my remarks more particularly now to the young man who is to be the new minister of northern affairs and national resources. I represent a constituency that borders on the Northwest Territories,
724	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources and I know something about the resources of that great area. I hope the minister's department will not follow the pattern that has been followed so often in the past in developing natural resources, the pattern associated with the granting of large blocks of resources to certain interests by deed of gift. Then they say to those people who receive these deeds, "All we expect of you is development; if you give employment to our people that is all we expect of you".
So far as I am concerned I think that is the wrong kind of development, and I would not suggest that the minister is even thinking in those terms; at least I should hope not. There is another way of securing the development of these vast resources of the north country. I think the federal government should keep title to all the resources in that 40 per cent of Canada's total area, and should never part with them under any circumstances. Having the title to those resources vested in the federal government is in my judgment the best insurance that the development will be orderly and in the interests of all the people of Canada. We have proved that method of development in the province from which I come. Ever since 1935 our program has been one of development under private enterprise, but with the government retaining possession of the resources and not parting with them under any circumstances.
In my judgment that is the only way we can be sure the development will be orderly and in the interests of the people. It is the only way, to my mind, whereby conditions can be laid down by the owners and regulations applied by the owners to see that the development is done according to rules.
I do not mean by this that it is necessary for the government to enter into developmental work. Quite frankly I am of the opposite opinion. I think there is good opportunity for private enterprise to be directed into the area and given every incentive to develop resources on behalf of the people of Canada so that, under a system of leases, rentals and royalties, the people of this country can profit in dollars and cents as well as in the strength that will be added to this great country of ours.
So I say I am hoping the minister will study very carefully means by which he can keep his fingers on the development of those resources and see that they do not get out of hand; and, moreover, so he can ensure that there will be forthcoming to the treasury of Canada some income that will make it possible for the people of this country to enjoy the benefits of their resources. That is the position we have always taken, a position that is not at all new to this group.


I wish to say something about the strategic importance of the territories. Not only is it a land of great wealth and of tremendous possibilities, a land holding great attractions for the young people, but it is also a land of great strategic importance to the whole of the North American continent. Whoever controls the great northland-and I refer to control of all the territory and all the strategic places therein-will to a great extent control the whole of the continent of North America. For that reason we should be very careful how we enter upon the development of the Northwest Territories.
I think one of the great need's today is for transportation and communication facilities, as was outlined by my colleague from Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) this afternoon. I might point out that one of the very few connections with the Northwest Territories passes north and south through the northern part of the Peace River constituency which I have the honour to represent in the house. That highway begins at the town of Grknshaw on the Northern Alberta Railways and snakes its way northward through more than 200 miles of excellent farmland and forests and bushland to Hay River and Great Slave lake, which lies just across the northern boundary of Alberta in the territories.
This 200 miles of highway through the territory runs through an area that is fairly flat and presents no real problem whatsoever to highway or railway building. The present highway was built or thrust into that Hay River area across the border of the territories about 16 years ago by the combined efforts of the federal government and the government of Alberta.
Seventeen years ago, the year before the highway was started, there was only a winter trail for tractor trains passing through much of that 200 miles between Grimshaw and Hay River. Now the road is a well-travelled highway with a gravel surface; and over that highway a very large tonnage of heavy machinery and materials is carried every year into the great northern territory to help in the development of that area.
There are only two other means of transportation. Before the highway was thrust into the country 17 years ago there was heavy traffic on the Peace river itself, by boat and barge. I believe it was the Northern Transportation Company as well as the Hudson's Bay Company which operated barges on regular schedule into the north country. They hauled huge tonnages in and hauled the produce of the farmers out. I am referring to the farmers in the area around Fort Vermilion and the territory along the river.

However, that was a slow means of transportation, and during the winter months it could not be used. As a consequence air traffic became important. But in that area, Mr. Speaker, we are lacking in airport facilities. We need them in the worst way. Up to this time a heavy air traffic has been conducted largely by bush pilots who engage upon what they call hedge-hopping expeditions. In that area we do need airport facilities in the worst way, well developed facilities.
Then the country needs a railway. I have said that the land between Grimshaw and Hay River, which is not very far from Great Slave lake, is flat country in which there would be no real problem in connection with building a highway or a railway. It would seem to me an important project to build a railway in that area so as to link up the territory, not only to facilitate strategic development but also to develop the resources. Huge tonnages of very valuable metals are now coming out, but they have to be brought out in the most expensive way. I feel certain that in the next few years we are going to see the need multiplied many times over and a railway going into that territory. It is quite possible that it would not be a very expensive project.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has made a plea on behalf of the Eskimo. I suppose he did so chiefly because he noted from the section in the bill that Eskimo affairs are to be attached to the new department. I listened with great interest to what he had to say, and was in agreement with him. He suggested the Eskimo might react to education just as many Indians have, and that the very best educational facilities should be made available. However, I am not forgetting some of the things that were done among the Eskimos up in Alaska not so many years ago, when the United States government was prevailed upon to do some work there. They sent so-called experts into the Eskimo country. These experts were supposed to civilize the Eskimos, and I may say that there were some tragic results.
For the benefit of the young minister and any others in the house who may be thinking in terms of the superiority of the white man in the matter of knowledge, understanding and education, I shall point out one or two of them. Everyone knows that for many years the Eskimos have been skilful workers in ivory. They used primitive tools and instruments to do their carving. Though the work was slow, they persisted in it, and did a remarkably fine and artistic job. Very often the ivory products commanded high prices and returns. However, when the United States experts went up into the
Northern Affairs and National Resources Eskimo land to educate those people, they got them to come into certain centres of population and proceeded to teach them how to use electric styluses in the work of carving out their ivory trinkets and statues and that sort of thing, and then sent them with their new-found knowledge back to isolated igloos, hundreds of miles in many cases from any electric outlet, and expected they would be able to use their new knowledge. Of course it does not work out that way.
They found, as they went up amongst the Eskimos, that the practice had been for many, many years for the mothers to nurse their babies until they were about six years old. That was a practice unheard of amongst white people, to have a child up to six years of age nursing, so they undertook to teach the barbarians that it was not wise to follow this barbaric habit; that those youngsters should be taught to eat by themselves while they were yet young. So those enlightened nurses from the United States got the mothers to wean the babies when they were nine months or a year old. The consequence was that the children never developed any teeth. The reason was quite obvious. The only source of calcium on which the children could draw to produce teeth in their mouths was from the mothers' milk, and until the children were about six years of age they did not have a full set of fine baby teeth. The consequence of new enlightenment being spread amongst them was that instead of helping the barbarians of the north, they were enlightening them to their detriment.
In the course of educating these people we ought to take into consideration the possibility that maybe they can teach us a great many things. Another thing that comes to my mind is this, and this was given to me by one of the head physicians sent by the United States government up into the Eskimo land to help to civilize those people. He said the Eskimo have been habitual users of the contents of the stomachs of the musk-ox and the reindeer. It was their salad and the only salad that they ever had, because these animals go about cropping the buds and the little green shoots of the trees and the bushes.
But that was supposed to be a very bad habit; it was dirty; it was unsanitary, said the medical people who went up there as teachers, and they must not do that. The thing to do was to gather your own salad, though there are times in the winter when the Eskimo could not possibly gather these things. However, they took the advice of those who went in there to teach them and stopped using the contents of the stomachs of the musk-ox and the reindeer. The result was
726	HOUSE OF
Northern Affairs and National Resources that various, serious diseases developed amongst them and many of them were wiped out.
Oftentimes that is the kind of thing we do in our efforts to be helpful to what we think are primitive people. In our enlightened efforts to help the Eskimo we often impose upon them a lot of foolish ideas. What we should be doing up in that country is teaching the Eskimo to make the wisest possible use of the things that are at hand in their own land, and then we should learn from them how to live in that north country. They have survived in that country over many, many decades, and have survived well.
I think a word of warning of that kind is quite justified. I do not want to lengthen the debate, Mr. Speaker, but I want to tell the young minister that I am glad to see a young and vigorous Canadian in charge of the department of northern affairs and national resources. I hope he will accept the invitation of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Simmons) and visit the area. I invite him at that time to drive with me over the Grimshaw-Slave lake highway in the north and on to see the hon. member for Yukon.
I would like to go with him. I would like first to drive in through the entrance, the gateway to the great north country, the Hay river and Great Slave lake area. I would like him to enjoy the matchless hospitality of those northern pioneer people. He will never experience anything like it elsewhere in this great country. I would like him also to get a little bit bushed. You know, people get that way up in the north country. They get bushed, meaning they get so attached to the country and what it has to offer that they want to come back and see it often. I want him to enjoy the friendliness of the people up in that territory and see what it has to offer.
I would not suggest, however, that he take his wife along. I will tell him what happened to one family. A chap took his wife along on a nice trip up in that territory. I tell the minister there is something about the area.
I do not know whether it is the moonbeams or the night air or what, but it was not long after that young couple came back to Ottawa that they had a fine, bouncing baby boy. I do not know anything else to blame it on but the north country. I do suggest, however, that he accept our invitation.
I want to assure the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) tonight that I certainly wholeheartedly support the principle of this bill.
It is a step in the right direction. It marks a milestone in the history of the development of that great north country, which is a young man's country.

Most of our great mines have been found not too far distant from where this Pre-Cambrian shield emerges from the parklands of the western

prairies. I have often called the route running parallel to the Pre-Cambrian shield the Main street of the Canadian future.
If you look at a globe you will see that the shortest distance from Alaska to the industrial east is along this Main street, coming out at Winnipeg and then going southeast and east. Earlier I mentioned in this chamber that the railroad which now ends at Lynn Lake and which roughly parallels this Main street is in a good location to be continued to serve the area about which we have been speaking.

At the present time conditions in the world are such that we have not the funds available to develop these resources in the way we would like to see them developed. However, I hope the world situation will clear up in time for us to see that great country opened up and developed in the way all Canadians want to see it done.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for introducing this bill, which places great importance and emphasis upon northern development. lit is evident that he realizes the great and growing importance of our northland, and especially the urgent need of accelerated government participation in the affairs of the constituency which I have the honour (to represent in this house.
I wish also to congratulate the minister on his appointment to this department, and I am confident he will administer the affairs of the north effectively and diligently and while doing so will have regard to the great responsibility of this government toward the opening up of an area that has an enormous potential in mineral wealth, water power, and oil resources.
Northern Affairs and National Resources
While I am in a congratulating mood I wish also to take this opportunity to thank the government for providing a separate constituency for the Mackenzie River district; and to give credit where credit is due, we of Mackenzie River wish to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Simmons), for his assistance in this regard during the last parliament.
The Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories lies between the northern boundaries of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan on the south and the Arctic ocean on the north, and from the Yukon boundary on the west to the 102nd parallel on the east, a total area of 527,000 square miles. A large portion of this area lies within the PreCambrian shield and contains such famous gold mines as Giant Yellowknife and Rycon within the confines of the Yellowknife district, and the Consolidated Discovery mine in the Giauque. lake area.
You all know of the large part played by Eldorado Mining and Refining, situated on Great Bear lake, in the production of uranium which has played such an important part in the destiny not only of Canada but of the free world. Also within the district of Mackenzie River there are known deposits of lead and zinc at Pine Point, and on the east arm of Great Slave lake there is a uranium potential in that area which lies between Fort Rae and Port Radium, and between the east arm of Great Slave lake and lake Athabasca where Eldorado Mining and Refining are developing their second uranium find. There are also great copper deposits along the Arctic rim which some day will prove of great economic importance to the north and Canada in general. These deposits have been known for some time but the lack of transportation and hydroelectric facilities has hindered their development.
At this time I should like to suggest to the government that consideration be given to the extension of the railroad from Lynn Lake, Manitoba, in a northwesterly direction to the north shore of lake Athabasca, to the uranium fields now being developed by the crown-owned company, Eldorado Mining and Refining, Gunnar Gold and many other companies which have spent considerable money in opening up this vast area, thence northwesterly from that point to Pine Point where there are great lead and zinc deposits which have been explored and developed by Consolidated Mining and Smelting, and thence southerly to Grimshaw, Alberta to connect with our present system of railroads in Canada.

It is gratifying to note that the minister is charged also with the responsibility of coordinating the activities of the several departments of government in relation to northern affairs. In this connection I would respectfully suggest to the minister that consideration be given to the construction of a chain of airports throughout the north which will provide for the defence of the continent as well as the economic development of the north.
The house will be interested to learn that up to date there have been 500 oil and gas permits covering 25 million acres issued by the Department of Resources and Development.
It is also interesting to note that this bill enables a far more active part to be taken by the government in the welfare of the Eskimo people. These people, who have been called primitive and uncivilized by some writers, have intellectual and physical capabilities which in my opinion could be cultivated and put to the service of Canada, particularly in the defence of our far north. Who knows the Arctic better and who can stand its rigorous conditions better than the Eskimos? In my opinion the Eskimos would make an ideal ground defence force in the event of invasion from the north.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up any more of the time of this house, but I hope to deal with more of the problems of my constituency when this bill reaches the committee stage.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has brought into the discussion the matter of power development. I think hon. members will agree with me that in the particular age in which we are living, a very scientific age and one in which a good deal of industrial expansion is going on, the matter of power development is extremely important. With the north country opening up, and with the minister giving some special attention to the development of the north country, this becomes very important by reason of the fact that in that country we have vast rivers and streams and great possibilities so far as power development is concerned.
But I should like to venture this suggestion to the minister. It does occur to me, and perhaps it is the old question of the chicken and the egg, that it is a case of whether population follows development or whether development follows population. It seems to me that we must give consideration to that particular point. We know that the north country is rich in natural resources, but so are other areas of the country where people have already settled rich in natural resources. Yet by very reason of these riches many of these natural resources are still left in the ground.
Northern Affairs and National Resources
I remember talking some time ago to an official of one of our largest coal mining companies. He pointed to a large map of the province of Alberta and the Northwest Territories on the wall. He pointed to the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains and the foothills. He said, "Mr. Hansell, in these hills all the way up to this northern part there are so many millions"-he may have said billions; I do not know-"of tons of coal". He said this coal was capable of taking care of a population of anywhere from 30 to 50 million people for many generations to come. The coal is there. There are less than a million people in Alberta to whom coal is supplied. Yet the coal mining industry there is pretty well going bankrupt. It is on its last legs because of the development of the diesel engine and because of the vast quantities of oil and gas that have been found there.
I am sure we are all in favour of the bill. I am sure we are all desirous of having the north country opened up, but it takes money and population to do so. I happen to have on my desk some printed matter which refers to an article in a publication known as Monogram, which I believe is put out by the Canadian General Electric Company. The article is written by J. L. McKeever, manager of the engineering apparatus division of that company. He refers to the St. Lawrence project and other developments in Canada, and I want to read a squib or two from his article. He says:
First, there is the problem of transmission of large blocks of power. So far in North America, 300 miles is about the longest transmission distance. However, in Sweden lines have greatly exceeded this length.
We may be able to have a great power development in the north, but it will cost a tremendous amount of money to put high tension wires through to the places where industry may see fit to invest its millions. Later he goes on to say:
. . . in special cases, where being near to power sources is more important than being near markets and materials, we may have to bring industry and population to the source of power. This was the case with the development of the tremendous aluminum industry in the Arvida region of Quebec, and it continues with the Kitimat development in British Columbia and the projected giant power scheme in the Yukon.
Then there is this little squib from the same article:
Whatever happens, it is imperative that if Canadian industry continues to expand at its present rate, our power generation must keep pace. This power will be obtained from whatever sources are most economical and feasible at the time.
