The particular point in this
section which interests me relates to tourist information. A short while ago some reference was made to the fact that we did not want the Northwest Territories developed. I do not think very many in this house feel that way at all. I am sure the hon. member for Macleod does not feel that way. However, there is a particular point here that is of interest to each and every Canadian citizen in the south. We have a very large tourist traffic that should be given consideration by this government.
I refer specifically to a business that netted Canada approximately $12 million last year. We in the southwestern part of British Columbia have a very fine port of entry at Douglas, but we find that one of the poorest features happens to be that there is no tourist bureau there which can give information either about the northern part of British Columbia or, in fact, any other part. Let me tell you that thousands of people come from the United States on any holiday in that country. I happen to have a store on the trans-Canada highway, and I know that on one of those holidays there was a line-up of cars for 14 miles coming into the city of New Westminster from the United States.
Most of those were United States cars. Those people had come to Canada to see the features of our country in which they would be interested. I find in talking to these visitors from day to day that they say they do not know where to go. I suggest to the minister of this new department that he might arrange to place one of the red-coated members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in that area, one who would know something about our great northland, our hunting and fishing, and could recommend places to go. That would be a very important factor so far as we are concerned. We know we are missing millions of dollars because those who are visiting us do not know what can be done if they enter our country as tourists.
I suggest further that this same tourist information bureau could give publicity to a national dish for each province. In the case of British Columbia it might be barbecued salmon. And let me tell you that you have not tasted anything until you have tasted barbecued salmon. Such a publicity feature could do the same thing for each part of Canada, including the northern section. I feel that by doing this we would create more interest in the minds of people living to the south of us, who are only too happy to come here and spend their money.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to have some explanation as to why it is deemed advisable to place Eskimo affairs under one department and Indian affairs under another, since both are in the north country and both have many similarities and are subject to similar problems. I realize, of course, that there are clear differences between their present status and the way in which they live.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
I shall try to reply briefly. The Leader of the Opposition is right to this extent, that both these peoples have problems in common. The Eskimos are not subject to a special act of parliament, and are not under a department of government with respect to their daily lives. I do not see anything in this bill which would indicate that that was the intention. On the other hand Indian affairs are, and since 1872 have been, under a statute which does direct in many ways the life of the Indian.


For that reason, since the Department of Citizenship and Immigration was established we have not thought it advisable to deal with Eskimos. They are not dealt with under a special act; and' because practically all of them live in the Northwest Territories we have felt that they might more properly be the responsibility of the minister who has the administration of that area.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not wish to pursue this matter unnecessarily, but I would point out the fact that Eskimo affairs are dealt with as a specified subject, that the name in itself recognizes that no matter how different the status of the Eskimo may be from that of the Indian, the fact remains that they have no organized municipalities or anything of that nature which provide them with a local educational system or other local facilities.
While it is perfectly true that they are not under any treaty arrangement or anything of that nature, nevertheless there is a tremendous responsibility resting upon the government to provide education. Many things must be done if the Eskimos are to be brought to the full status of citizenship.
In saying that I recognize once again that the Eskimos are accorded the privilege of voting, and that they have other privileges withheld from those Indians who avail themselves of treaty rights. Nevertheless I must repeat what I said before, that I see many similarities, particularly in the northland where the Eskimos and the Indians live fairly close together.

Yes; I have been through there. When you go through the Dogrib country you go into the Eskimo country, and it is the same in other parts of the northland. They do not live in the same areas but they do live in adjacent areas. The hunting area of the Dogribs extends to the Eskimo country.
All I am pointing out is that anybody who is trying to carry out health or educational measures or anything of that kind in that area might be going into the Eskimo country and doing the same sort of thing. I have pointed out that this new measure makes reference to Eskimo affairs, and I am suggesting that the problems to be tackled will have many similarities with Indian affairs, although there are fundamental differences relating to the treaty rights of the Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTITUTION OF DEPARTMENT, DEFINITION OF DUTIES AND FUNCTIONS OF MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
So there will be no misunderstanding, the essential difference is that if there are complaints against the administration of Indian affairs it has been over the reserve system. Whether that is a correct or

an incorrect criticism, we ought to agree that we do not want to start imposing upon the Eskimo people as such any of the restrictions, if you like, now imposed on the Indians. But with respect to the medical services there, of course, they are administered by the other department and are available to both groups.
However, what the Leader of the Opposition has said is undoubtedly true, that the problems of dealing with these people are much similar, in that their background is common, and their standard of education is as high as all the others. Certainly every effort will be made, I am confident, by the minister in charge of this department to see that the Eskimos are given treatment on a standard comparable to that of the white people in the Northwest Territories. It is for that reason that I am particularly pleased that he should have charge of the Eskimo problem as such, in order to have it dealt
Northern Affairs and National Resources with in common with all those in the Northwest Territories.
